Denial and restriction of services

164. Entities that have not submitted their beneficial ownership information are restricted from accessing services such as filing of amendments or any resolutions at BIPA. In addition, such entities cannot be issued certificates of good standing.
165. Secondly, BIPA has collaborated with the Financial Intelligence Centre (FIC) and Bank of Namibia to restrict banking services to non-compliant entities.

166. In April 2024, the FIC issued Directive 01 of 2024, under its powers contained in the FIA, to strengthen national efforts to increase the submission of beneficial ownership information to BIPA. This intervention followed concerns regarding the low rate of beneficial ownership filings with BIPA. The FIC directive was to complement the efforts being undertaken by BIPA. Further, the FIC directive specifically sought to leverage the banking sector as part of a broader, multifaceted national strategy to increase beneficial ownership compliance.

167. The aim of this collaborative measure was to incentivise compliance by linking beneficial ownership compliance to continued access to banking services. Banks were instructed to obtain the periodically updated beneficial ownership-inactive list published by BIPA (see paragraph 173) and identify any of their clients appearing on this list. Banks were required to notify and remind such clients to submit their outstanding beneficial ownership information to BIPA and provide proof of filing to their bank. In cases where companies or close corporations failed to update their beneficial ownership information as required by law, banks were directed to restrict access to banking services, including withdrawals and transfers of funds or assets, until compliance was achieved.

168. Namibia reported that these enforcement actions have improved the rate of compliance. Regarding the restriction on banking services, the FIC conducted targeted inspections of all seven banks in 2025 to assess compliance with its directive. The inspections found that banks had largely implemented the required measures, although the authorities did not confirm that any banks were sanctioned for failing to implement the directive. The representatives of banks interviewed during the on-site visit confirmed that they had implemented FIC's directive and asked their customers to present letters of good standing from BIPA, prior to accessing banking services.

text: Publishing of inactive entities

173. Companies and close corporations that persistently fail to comply with the beneficial ownership requirements are placed on an inactive list and are subsequently subject to deregistration after six months (s. 122A(15), Companies Act and s. 16A(15), CC Act). This list is published on the BIPA website. $^{14}$ The list published as of 6 February 2025 contains 144 576 entities, most of which are close corporations. The risk posed to availability of beneficial ownership information by inactive close corporations is of reduced materiality (see paragraph 178).

174. The Namibian authorities explained that the inactive list is useful for reference purposes by the competent authority, in EOIR cases. When a request for beneficial ownership information is received, the competent authority first checks to determine whether the entity subject to the request is published on the inactive list, before proceeding to send the notice for collection of the requested information to BIPA or to an AML-obliged person (see further discussions under Element B.1).

175. Namibia has categorised such listed entities for deregistration, although this has not been carried out yet. BIPA has issued notices to the effect that such entities would be de-registered starting 16 May 2025, although this deadline was further extended until early 2026. De-registrations are now set to commence. As of 16 February 2026, BIPA issued a notice of deregistration for the first tranche of 699 close corporations that have since been deregistered. Deregistered entities cease to exist (see paragraphs 67 and 68).

176. Namibian authorities explained that most of these entities are close corporations that have not yet commenced any business operations. As discussed in the paragraph 99, the Namibian authorities explained that the government of Namibia periodically introduces financial empowerment initiatives that encourage citizens to create formal legal entities. However, many of these entities never become operational and were established to position themselves to secure tenders or other government-supported opportunities.

177. The authorities further reported that during the inspections on the implementation of FIC Directive 01 of 2024 (see paragraph 168), an estimated 14 384 entities on the inactive list (representing about 10% of the inactive population) were identified as having bank accounts in Namibia and the majority of these have since complied. It was further established that the remaining 130 782 entities (around 90%), most of which are close corporations, did not have bank accounts in Namibian banks. BIPA additionally noted that 70 to 80% of these non-compliant entities did not have any recent filings with the registrar, further confirming the possibility that such entities may not have ongoing business transactions. However, there is still the possibility that such entities may conduct business outside of Namibia.

179. These activities have improved the rate of filing of beneficial ownership information to BIPA. Anti-money laundering law – Accountable institutions (AML-obliged persons) and customer due diligence

180. The AML framework (see paragraph 31) requires AML-obliged persons, termed as accountable institutions, to identify and verify the identity of their clients, identify the beneficial owners of such clients and take reasonable measures to verify the identity of the beneficial owners using reliable source documents (FIA, s. 21(2)). This obligation applies before establishing a business relationship and before concluding certain transactions.

181. If the AML-obliged person is unable to verify the customer's identity or complete the CDD process, the business relationship cannot be established. If there is an already established and ongoing business relationship, the AML-obliged person must terminate the relationship and file a suspicious transaction report to the FIC.

182. The Financial Intelligence Regulations, hereafter termed as the FI Regulations, require that for the identification of beneficial owners, the AML-obliged persons must obtain the following information: i) full name and previous names if any, ii) nationality, iii) national identity number, iv) passport number or v) date of birth in case of a minor (Regulation 6). The representatives of AML-obliged persons interviewed during the on-site visit explained that the identities of individuals are cross-checked against submitted identity documents.

183. AML-obliged persons are also obliged to conduct CDD that is aligned to the risk profile of the client. Section 20A(4) of the FIA requires AML-obliged persons to develop, adopt and implement internal policies to effectively manage and mitigate risks.

184. The beneficial ownership guidance note (see paragraph 117) explains that the risk assessment of a client with regard to money laundering or terrorism financing is the starting point before CDD is conducted and that it should be documented in the client's file or in the relevant client onboarding systems. Depending on the risk profile of the client, the AML-obliged person may conduct simplified, standard or enhanced due diligence. Simplified CDD can only be conducted in circumstances where there is no suspicion of money laundering or terrorism financing. Regardless of the category of due diligence conducted, the AML-obliged person must identify the client, its beneficial owners and maintain such information (s. 24, FIA).

185. AML-obliged persons must continuously review any complex, unusually large, or otherwise unusual transactions that have no clear lawful purpose. They must also apply enhanced due diligence to clients and transactions linked to higher-risk countries identified by institutional, national Financial Action Task Force (FATF) assessments.

186. Regarding the updating of CDD and beneficial ownership information on existing clients, AML-obliged persons are required to conduct ongoing due diligence throughout the business relationship, including maintaining up-to-date client and beneficial ownership information, and monitoring transactions to ensure they align with the customer's profile. Further, enhanced CDD should be conducted where there are doubts on the veracity of the previously obtained customer identification data or if there is suspicion of money laundering or terrorism financing, regardless of the risk posed by the client. To facilitate this approach, AML-obliged persons must develop and implement internal policies that are consistent with the national or sectoral money laundering or terrorism financing risk assessments (s. 20A and 24, FIA). The FIA only requires that for high-risk clients, the CDD measures should be applied more frequently to ensure that information is up to date (see paragraph 353).

187. Guidance note no. 4 of 2009 on the Implementation of a Compliance Regime requires AML-obliged persons to review CDD at least once every year for high-risk clients and at least once in two years for all other clients. This guidance is binding and enforceable by the authorities. Namibian authorities explained that in practice AML-obliged persons have adopted specified frequencies of at least every year for high-risk clients, at least every two years and at least every three to five years for medium and low risk clients, respectively. The authorities nonetheless consider the range of these frequencies to be appropriate. Moreover, the authorities can sanction an AML-obliged person if the internal policy set is deemed inappropriate. The Nambian authorities explained that in practice, all the seven banks operating in Namibia have set appropriate frequencies to update CDD and beneficial ownership information. In other cases, AML-obliged persons (mainly TCSPs) have been sanctioned for setting inappropriate frequencies or failing to adhere to the frequencies set in their internal policies (see paragraph 205). Since AML-obliged persons may set frequencies that depart from what is included in the binding guidance, there is a potential risk depending on what type of frequencies all AML-obliged persons will set.

188. Regarding the availability of beneficial ownership information on companies and close corporations, any potential gap is mitigated by the requirements to update the beneficial ownership information submitted to BIPA, at least annually. Considering that AML-obliged persons may set frequencies in their internal policies that differ from those stated in the guidance, Namibia should align the provisions of the binding guidance and the practice by AML-obliged persons to ensure that CDD and beneficial ownership information are updated appropriately for all entities and arrangements (see Annex 1).

189. AML-obliged persons are obliged to maintain detailed information concerning the CDD activities conducted, including any document obtained to verify the identity of the client or beneficial owner and the nature of transactions conducted. The records related to the establishment of a business relationship must be kept throughout the course of the business relationship and thereafter, for five years from the date the business relationship is terminated, or longer if required by the authorities.

190. If an AML-obliged person ceases to exist, the records will be maintained by the liquidator as discussed in the paragraphs 72 to 73. If a liquidator who is a natural person dies, the rules governing the administration of deceased persons as governed by the MOHC would apply in ensuring that the estate of the deceased person is properly managed.

191. An AML-obliged person may rely on a third party to carry out CDD and to introduce business to them (Regulation 5, FI regulations). In those circumstances, the AML-obliged person must satisfy itself that the third party or introducer is subject to regulation, supervision, monitoring or equivalent compliance measures relating to CDD and record-keeping and is sufficiently knowledgeable and resourced to ensure compliance. Further, the AML-obliged person is obliged to immediately obtain the identification information of the client, which includes, at a minimum, the beneficial owners of the client. The AML-obliged person must also satisfy themselves that the third party can provide copies of all identification data and documentation without delay upon request. When an AML-obliged person relies on another institution or a third party for customer identification and verification, the ultimate responsibility for ensuring that proper CDD is conducted remains with the AML-obliged person. The representatives of the AML-obliged persons met during the on-site visit, and the supervisory agencies explained that where reliance is placed on third parties, these requirements were fully met. These conditions are in line with the standard.

Anti-money laundering law requirements – oversight and enforcement

192. The FIA contains both administrative and criminal sanctions that can be applied against non-compliant AML-obliged persons or any other persons. Any person has failed to comply with the provisions of the FIA, any regulation or directive, is liable to administrative sanctions that comprise, i) caution not to repeat the conduct, ii) reprimand, iii) directive to take remedial action, iv) restriction or suspension of certain business activities, v) suspension of licence or a financial penalty not exceeding NAD 10 million (EUR 452 570) (s. 56(3), FIA).

193. Further, an AML-obliged person who does not perform CDD and identify the beneficial owners of its clients as prescribed by the AML framework commits an offence and is liable to a fine not exceeding NAD 100 million (EUR 4.5 million), and if the commission of the offence is attributable to a representative of the AML-obliged person, then such representative is liable to a fine or imprisonment not exceeding 30 years, or to both (s. 24(3), FIA). The same penalty applies to an AML-obliged person who does not maintain CDD and beneficial ownership records as required (s. 26(4), FIA).

194. The FIC and the Namibia Financial Institutions Supervisory Authority (NAMFISA) are mandated to supervise the implementation of AML requirements by AML-obliged persons. The FIC supervises the banking sector and non-financial AML-obliged persons, while NAMFISA supervises the non-banking financial sector.

195. In executing their supervisory mandates, both the FIC and NAMFISA employ risk-based approaches. Both institutions have developed supervision methodologies that are relied upon to conduct oversight, supervision and enforcement.
Supervision by the Namibia Financial Intelligence Centre

196. As discussed at paragraphs 32 and 33, Namibia has been working to address the deficiencies identified in its 2022 FATF Mutual Evaluation Report, and to this end, the FIC has updated its supervision methodology and enhanced its supervision and sanctioning since 2023. The FIC conducts regular compliance monitoring activities, which include reviewing periodic reports submitted by AML-obliged persons, considering information received from external sources that is likely to affect the compliance behaviour of AML-obliged persons, and continuously assessing risks at the sectoral and national levels. The FIC also provides training to AML-obliged persons to ensure proper understanding and implementation of all AML obligations.

197. The FIC's compliance assessment and supervision methodology was first developed in 2016 and is regularly updated. Based on its supervision methodology, the FIC prepares an annual plan that prioritises sectors and entities with a high risk of non-compliance. The annual plan identifies sectors and AML-obliged persons scheduled for supervisory activities in the given year and outlines the type and depth of planned examinations. Coordination with other regulatory and supervisory bodies is incorporated into the planning process to avoid duplication. For example, the FIC conducts joint assessments with other prudential regulatory authorities.

A.1.2 Bearer shares

213. Prior to July 2023, companies could issue share warrants to bearer with respect to a registered share in the register of members. The holders of such shares could only exercise their rights in the company upon depositing the share warrant at the company's premises. On 21 July 2023, amendments to the Companies Act abolished the issuance of share warrants to bearer.

214. Section 108(4) of the Companies Act provides that where a company had issued a share warrant to a bearer before 21 July 2023, the bearer must, within 30 days, convert the share warrant into an ordinary par value share. Further, for any share warrants not converted within the prescribed timeframe, the bearer would be liable to a fine not exceeding NAD 40 (EUR 1.8) for every day that the non-compliance continues.

215. Eventually, on 7 November 2023, the registrar issued a directive indicating that any share warrant to bearer not converted by 30 November 2023 would be considered null and void and all associated rights with such warrants lost. Further, there is no possibility to revive any of such rights or otherwise seek compensation. In addition, the bearer that still holds such shares would still be liable to the daily monetary penalty stated in paragraph 214 above. The directive further instructed all financial institutions, legal practitioners and stockbrokers not to conduct any transactions that involve share warrants to bearer.

216. Since a share warrant could only be issued in respect of an already registered share, Namibian authorities reported that the data stored at BIPA does not facilitate an effective check; however, the authorities are not aware of any companies that could have issued share warrants to bearer in the past. In any case, the issuance of share warrants to bearer is now prohibited. Any share warrants to bearer that were not converted are now lost and their holders cannot exercise any rights with the company. Further, owing to the self-enforcing nature of legal ownership rights in a company, it is incumbent upon the holder of the share warrant to ensure that its right to a share has been captured in the register of members, otherwise such a right would revert to the shareholder previously listed in the register. The registers of members of companies identify all the legal owners of the company except in situations of nominee arrangements (see paragraphs 83 to 87).

A.1.3 Partnerships
Types of partnerships

217. Partnerships in Namibia are legal arrangements without legal personality. There is no legislation governing the incorporation, registration or formation of partnerships in Namibia. As such, only general partnerships created by a contractual agreement between the partners in accordance with common law principles can be formed.

218. The income of partnerships is taxed at the level of the partners, while partnerships themselves must account for VAT and/or pay as you earn deductions made on employee remunerations. Accordingly, all partnerships carrying on business in Namibia must be registered with NamRA for tax purposes. There were 1 219 partnerships registered with NamRA as of 30 September 2025. Namibia further reported that 1 098 partnerships were identified as having active bank accounts with Namibian banks. Most of the legal practice work in Namibia is conducted under partnerships. The representatives of banks and lawyers confirmed that every legal practitioner who holds or receives money on behalf of another person is obliged to open a trust banking account. This requirement has also contributed to the high prevalence of bank accounts of partnerships in Namibia. Namibian authorities explained that the remaining 121 partnerships (10%) were related to an ongoing register cleaning exercise at NamRA.
Identity information

219. Identity information of partnerships is mainly available through tax and the AML laws. Further, although partnerships themselves have no legal obligations to maintain identity information of their partners, since partnerships are contractual arrangements between two or more persons or entities involved together in a business venture, the identity of partners to the arrangement should be known to the other partner(s), through the partnership agreement or otherwise.

220. Regarding tax law obligations, persons operating under a partnership that carry on business in Namibia or otherwise become liable for any tax, must register and submit returns to NamRA. Section 56(16) of the Income Tax Act (ITA) requires partners to submit separate income tax returns for each of the partners. Moreover, to register as an individual taxpayer, copies of the Namibian national identity card, Namibian passport and a copy of the driver's licence must be submitted. For non-Namibian citizens, a certified copy of the passport or asylum permit must be submitted. Consequently, the identity information on participants in a partnership is available with NamRA.

221. Additionally, as explained in paragraph 214, 90% of the partnerships registered with NamRA have bank accounts in Namibia. The representatives of the banks met during the on-site visit explained that in practice, banks strictly require partnerships to provide copies of partnership agreements before bank accounts are opened. Therefore, the identity information of a partnership shall also be available to banks (see additional discussion on beneficial ownership).
Beneficial ownership information

222. The AML framework is the only source of beneficial ownership information on partnerships in Namibia. However, there is no obligation in the legal and regulatory framework requiring all partnerships to engage an AML-obliged person in an ongoing business relationship. In practice, most partnerships have a bank account with a Namibian bank (see paragraph 217).

223. The FIA definition of beneficial owner as discussed in paragraph 109 applies to partnerships as well, with the exception that reference to “a legal person” in clause (b)(i) is replaced with “a partnership”.

In Namibia, partnerships are legal arrangements and in such a case, the standard requires that all the parties to the partnership and any natural person(s) who exercise control over the partnership be identified. Moreover, all the partners may be involved in decision making and management of the partnership, regardless of the percentage of their capital contributions or percentage of participation in the partnership.

226. While the definition refers to a 25% threshold of ownership interest, the main part of the definition as stated in paragraph 223 requires a simultaneous application of the criteria of ownership and control, and as such, would lead to the identification of all the partners in a partnership. Additionally, the FIC guidance note explains that for general partnerships, all partners should be considered as beneficial owners due to their direct involvement in the management and control of the partnership. Consequently, the definition and method contained in the FIA and the FIC guidance note facilitate the identification of beneficial owners in line with the standard.

A.1.4 Trusts

234. Trusts are recognised in Namibia and can be administered under the Trust Administration Act (TAA). All trusts established in Namibia are required to register with the Master of the High Court (MOHC), trusts division and all trustees of Namibian trusts (whether acting in professional or non-professional capacity) must be authorised by and registered with the MOHC (s. 8, TAA). The MOHC is a directorate under the Ministry of Justice and Labour Relations.
235. The following types of trusts can be created in Namibia:

\- Inter-vivos trusts – trusts that are established whilst the founder is still alive and assets are donated to the trust for the benefit of beneficiaries. Beneficiaries may be identified or may be discretionary. Inter-vivos trusts are further subdivided into business trusts, family trusts, non-profit trusts and special vehicle trusts. There were 9 860 inter-vivos trusts registered in Namibia as of 30 September 2025.

\- Testamentary trusts – trusts established in accordance with the instructions contained in a last will and testament of a deceased person. These govern the disposition of the property of a deceased person. There were 341 testamentary trusts registered in Namibia as of 30 September 2025.

236. Foreign trusts are also required to register with the MOHC (s. 8, TAA). The TAA defines foreign trusts as trusts created or registered in another jurisdiction that contain trust property located in Namibia. In the case of these foreign trusts (with trust property located in Namibia), at least one Namibian citizen or permanent resident must be appointed as a trustee.

The definition of foreign trusts contained in the TAA does not cover the situation where a foreign trust arrangement that does not contain property located in Namibia, is administered by a trustee resident in Namibia. Requirements to maintain identity and beneficial information in relation to trusts and implementation in practice
Identity information

238. The information identifying the persons that are parties to the trust arrangement and the beneficial ownership information of the trust is available from a combination of common law obligations on trustees, tax law obligations, trust administration obligations contained in the TAA and the requirements related to the identification of beneficial ownership contained in the TAA and the AML framework.

239. Under the common law, a trust is created by a settlor who may appoint the trustees. The common law obligations require trustees to have full knowledge of all the trust documents, act in the best interests of the beneficiaries and only distribute assets to the beneficiaries of the trust. Therefore, it is expected that these obligations can result in the trustee holding identity information on all trustees, settlor and beneficial owners (e.g. settlor(s) and the beneficiaries who are natural persons) to carry out the trustee's duties.

240. Further, any trust that becomes liable for any tax or becomes liable to submit any return is required to register for tax purposes and file tax returns with NamRA (s. 1 and 56 (1), ITA); see paragraphs 24 and 291). Pursuant to this requirement, 6 205 trusts are registered with NamRA. The ITA defines a trustee in a comprehensive manner and the definition includes anyone acting in private or official capacity and as such would cover both professional and non-professional trustees resident in Namibia. Trustees are responsible for the registration and filing of tax returns with respect to trusts. In some cases, the ITA requires that trustees register for tax purposes, as employers (s. 15 and 16). The registration for tax purposes requires the submission of identity information on the parties to a trust to NamRA.

241. Regarding trust administration obligations, the TAA (s. 8) requires that trust instruments of Namibian trusts and foreign trusts that contain property located in Namibia be registered with the MOHC. The trust instrument must be notarised, and for a foreign trust, the instrument must be certified by the authority of an official authorised in the jurisdiction of establishment.
242. The trust instrument must contain the following information:
• on the trust: the type of trust, its objects and the trust property
• identity and beneficial ownership: the trustee(s), beneficial owners.

243. The instrument should be accompanied by a written acceptance from the trustee to act in such a capacity. It should also be accompanied by an undertaking from an accountant or auditor to act as the accountant or auditor of the trust.

244. In addition, the trustee is obliged to keep the trust instrument and any other document that contains the terms of trust. The trustee must also maintain up-to-date records on the founder (full names and national identification number), beneficiaries (full names, identification and passport numbers) and information identifying all trustees; s. 20(1), TAA). The identity documents of the parties, such as passports and other identity documents for individuals, and incorporation documents where the parties are legal persons, must be submitted to the MOHC.
GLOBAL FORUM ON TRANSPARENCY AND EXCHANGE OF INFORMATION FOR TAX PURPOSES: NAMIBIA 2026 (SECOND ROUND) © OECD 2026
Beneficial ownership requirements – Trust Administration Act

245. Regarding beneficial ownership information requirements, the TAA requires a trustee of a Namibian trust or relevant foreign trust to establish and record the beneficial ownership information of the trust (s. 22, TAA). The TAA directs that the definition of beneficial owner contained in the FIA is also applicable for purposes of the TAA. The definition as captured in paragraphs 109 and 223 applies to trusts as well, with the exception that reference to “a legal person” in clause (b)(i) is replaced with “a trust or other legal arrangement”.
246. Further, schedule 5 of the FIA and the guidance note issued by the FIC explain the methods for the identification of beneficial owners of a trust or similar arrangement. It states that:
In relation to a trust -
(a) the settlor;
(b) a trustee;
(c) a protector, if any;
(d) a natural person who is a beneficiary of a trust or a class of beneficiaries if the individuals benefiting from the trust are yet to be determined;
(e) any other natural person exercising ultimate control over the trust by other means; or

(f) any other natural person exercising ultimate effective control over a trust by means of direct or indirect ownership or by other means, such that when the person acts alone or jointly with another person or with the consent of another person, the person has ultimate power to –
(i) dispose of, advance, lend, invest, pay or apply trust property;
(ii) vary or terminate the trust;
(iii) add or remove a person as a beneficiary or as a class of beneficiaries of the trust;
(iv) appoint or remove a trustee or give another person control over the trust; or
(v) direct, withhold consent or overrule the exercise of a power referred to in subparagraphs (i) to (iv).

247. The definition requires the identification of all parties to a trust in accordance with the standard. In addition, it states that any other natural person who has ultimate effective control of the trust should be identified. Moreover, it explains that direct and indirect control and whether the person is acting alone or jointly should be considered. Finally, it lists examples of control in clause (f) while clause (e) already provides that any other means of control should be considered.

248. To supplement the definition and methodology of identification of beneficial ownership of trusts as contained in the FIA, the FIC guidance note explains that for trusts, where legal persons hold the positions of the parties to a trust, then the beneficial owners of such persons must be identified. This would ensure looking through the parties of the trust.

249. Every trustee is mandated to keep a register of parties to the trust and a register of beneficial owners of the trust, and to submit such information to the MOHC. The trustee must verify that the beneficial ownership information submitted to MOHC is accurate, adequate and up to date. For each beneficial owner, the information that must be maintained includes:

\- full names and any former names; for a Namibian citizen, the date of birth and national identity number; for non-citizens, the passport number
\- addresses and telephone contacts – residential, business, email and postal addresses and telephone contacts
\- nationality
\- date indicating the beginning and conclusion of beneficial ownership and nature and extent of beneficial ownership.
250. A trustee must keep certified copies of all the identity documents (Regulation 7, TAA Regulations).

251. The trustee is obliged to submit the beneficial ownership of the trust to the MOHC at the time of registration. Any changes to the reported beneficial ownership must be reported within 14 days (s. 22, TAA). In addition, the trustee must submit annual declarations of beneficial ownership to the MOHC.
252. The identity and beneficial ownership information maintained by the trustee should be kept for at least five years from the date of termination of the trust or longer if required (s. 26, TAA).
Beneficial ownership requirements – Anti-money laundering law

253. Regarding AML obligations, trustees in Namibia have obligations to conduct CDD and identify the beneficial ownership information of the trust. The definition discussed above and the additional guidance contained in the FIC guidance note (see paragraphs 246 to 248) apply to trustees while conducting CDD and identifying the beneficial ownership information of trusts.

254. AML-obliged persons are required to update beneficial ownership information whenever there is a change and/or to review and update CDD and beneficial ownership information at least once every year for high-risk clients and at least one in two years for all other clients. In practice, AML-obliged persons have to set frequencies in their internal policies, which may slightly depart from the regulatory guidance, however, the authorities require that such frequencies still be appropriate. Namibian authorities have sanctioned AML-obliged persons for not setting appropriate policies or not following them (paragraphs 185 and 186). For trusts, any potential gap is mitigated by the requirements on trustees to update the information submitted to MOHC within 14 days of change and through annual returns. Considering that AML-obliged persons may set frequencies in their internal policies that differ from those stated in the guidance, Namibia should align the provisions of the binding guidance and the practice by AML-obliged persons to ensure that CDD and beneficial ownership information are updated appropriately for all trusts (see Annex 1).
Oversight and enforcement
255. The oversight and enforcement framework described under section A.1.1 also applies to trusts.

256. Regarding the submission of beneficial ownership information to the MOHC, awareness and sensitisation activities were conducted in tandem with BIPA. The trusts that have not submitted their beneficial ownership information are administratively classified by the MOHC as being inactive. The MOHC has issued various directives since 2023 to require the submission of beneficial ownership information, utilisation of trust practitioners that are registered and the deregistration of trusts that have not submitted beneficial ownership information. To this end, 815 trusts that were inactive have since been deregistered and 63% of all the registered trusts have submitted their beneficial ownership information. When a trust is deregistered, the trust property is distributed as per the trust deed and if no beneficiaries were identified, the trust property will vest in the government.

257. Namibian authorities reported that the MOHC conducts checks on the submitted beneficial ownership information. The MOHC checks that only notarised and certified (for non-Namibian citizens) identity information is submitted. No further qualitative or completeness checks have been performed on the submitted information yet. Namibia is recommended to strengthen its supervision and enforcement actions to ensure the availability of adequate, accurate and up-to-date beneficial ownership information of trusts (including inactive ones) in all cases, in line with the standard.
GLOBAL FORUM ON TRANSPARENCY AND EXCHANGE OF INFORMATION FOR TAX PURPOSES: NAMIBIA 2026 (SECOND ROUND) © OECD 2026

258. Regarding the AML obligations, the oversight and enforcement activities conducted by the FIC and NAMFISA also cover trustees and trust practitioners (see paragraph 138). The FIC guidance note was recently improved in 2025. The authorities have already started supervising the implementation of the recent changes, although it was not clear that non-financial AML-obliged persons fully understood and applied CDD measures effectively. Namibia is recommended to continue to monitor the implementation of recent changes in the guidance for identification of beneficial owners to ensure that adequate, accurate and up-to-date beneficial ownership information of all trusts is available in all cases.
Availability of trust information in EOIR practice

259. Namibia received five requests on beneficial ownership information of trusts, and in all cases, the requested information was provided to the requesting jurisdictions. Peers were satisfied with the responses obtained.
A.1.5 Foundations

260. Foundations can be established in Namibia as non-profit companies under section 21 of the Companies Act, as non-profit trusts under the TAA, or as welfare organisations under the National Welfare Act. In all situations, these foundations must pursue non-profit or public interest activities of a charitable, religious, cultural, educational, political, social, fraternal purpose or any other type of welfare activity intended to benefit the public or a section of the public. No portion of the foundation's income can be paid whether directly or indirectly to its members.

261. Therefore, foundations in Namibia are not relevant for EOIR purposes. In any case, these structures are closely monitored by the FIC to ensure that they are not misused for money laundering and terrorism financing purposes.
Other relevant entities and arrangements – co-operative societies

262. The formation and regulation of co-operatives is governed by the Co-operatives Act, which is administered by the Registrar of Co-operatives. Section 5 of the Co-operatives Act requires that all co-operatives be registered with the Registrar of Co-operatives. Co-operatives obtain legal personality upon registration (s. 17(1)(a), Co-operatives Act).

263. Co-operatives are either workers' co-operatives or service co-operatives. There were 23 workers co-operatives and 211 service co-operatives registered in Namibia as of 30 September 2025. Namibia reported that most co-operatives are in the agriculture sector (84% of all registered co-operatives).

264. The objective of a co-operative in Namibia is the promotion of the economic and social interests of its members by providing effective services to its members in accordance with sound business principles. There are three categories of co-operatives. Individuals and other persons may form a primary co-operative. The individuals must be citizens or ordinary residents in Namibia, while legal persons must be Namibian entities. Two or more primary co-operatives can form a secondary co-operative. Two or more secondary co-operatives may form a co-operative that would be at a higher level than a secondary co-operative (s. 10, Co-operatives Act). All the co-operatives in Namibia are primary co-operatives except one, which is a secondary co-operative. Once co-operatives reach a significant level of growth, $^{15}$ they are required to convert or transform into other legal entities, such as companies or close corporations.
GLOBAL FORUM ON TRANSPARENCY AND EXCHANGE OF INFORMATION FOR TAX PURPOSES: NAMIBIA 2026 (SECOND ROUND) © OECD 2026

265. Foreign co-operatives are permitted to operate in Namibia, but only upon registration. The foreign co-operative can only be permitted if at least one of its members is a Namibian co-operative, no foreign co-operative can be registered as a primary co-operative. In practice, there are no foreign cooperatives registered in Namibia.
Identity information on members

266. The information identifying the founding members of a co-operative must be submitted to the Registrar of Co-operatives at the time of registration. There are no further requirements for co-operatives to submit the information of their members to the Registrar of Co-operatives, which means that the registrar may not have up-to-date information on its membership. Nevertheless, robust identity information is maintained by the co-operatives themselves.

267. Co-operatives must keep a register of their members at their offices in Namibia. For each member, the register of members must contain the full names, identity number and address details. For legal entity members, the entity registration number must be included. All the rights of membership are drawn from the register of members (s. 20, Co-operatives Act) and thus, it is incumbent upon members to pursue their rights and be included on the register.

268. Additionally, co-operatives are registered with NamRA for tax purposes and must submit information on their members through the tax registration process. All co-operatives are taxable and must register with NamRA to account for income taxes, $^{16}$ VAT or pay as you earn deductions on employees. Co-operatives are required to include an updated list of their members in the financial statements submitted to NamRA for income tax reporting purposes. Therefore, the information identifying the members of a co-operative is also available at NamRA.
Beneficial ownership information

269. The beneficial ownership information of co-operatives is available through the AML framework. The Co-operative Societies Ordinance requires every co-operative to have a bank account into which all the money received by the co-operative must be deposited. The Namibian authorities confirmed that, in practice, only bank accounts from Namibian banks are accepted. Therefore, the availability of beneficial ownership information is ensured through the CDD obligations of banks.

270. The definition of beneficial owner discussed under section A.1.1 for legal entities also applies for co-operatives. As discussed in paragraphs 109 to 120, the definition and methods of identifying beneficial owners of legal entities are robust.

271. AML-obliged persons are required to update beneficial ownership information whenever there is a change and/or to review and update CDD and beneficial ownership information at least once every year for high-risk clients and at least one in two years for all other clients. In practice, AML-obliged persons have set frequencies in their internal policies. Namibian authorities have sanctioned AML-obliged persons for not setting appropriate policies or not following the internal policies (paragraphs 185 and 186). Considering that AML-obliged persons may set frequencies in their internal policies that differ from those stated in the guidance, Namibia should align the provisions of the binding guidance and the practice by

$^{15}$ The determination of growth is at the discretion of the Registrar of Co-operatives. Contributing factors include: the co-operative's operational scale, the amount of member benefits, and overall sustainability.
$^{16}$ Service co-operatives account for income taxes on surplus incomes left after the provision of shared services, while worker's co-operatives account for income taxes on their net profits.
GLOBAL FORUM ON TRANSPARENCY AND EXCHANGE OF INFORMATION FOR TAX PURPOSES: NAMIBIA 2026 (SECOND ROUND) © OECD 2026
AML-obliged persons to ensure that CDD and beneficial ownership information are updated appropriately for all co-operatives (see Annex 1).

272. A co-operative may cease to exist through dissolution and liquidation, amalgamation, transfer, division and conversion to other legal forms (ss. 73, 74, 76 and 77, Co-operatives Act). When a co-operative is amalgamated, transferred or converted, then the surviving or new co-operative retains the membership information of the extinguished co-operative. On the other hand, if the co-operative ceases to exist through dissolution and liquidation, the liquidator is obliged to hand over all the books and records of the co-operative to the Registrar of Co-operatives. Although the act is not explicit on how long the registrar should keep such records, Namibian authorities explained that in practice, all records submitted to the registrar are kept indefinitely.
Oversight and enforcement activities

273. The obligations to maintain identity information are mainly supervised through audits from the office of the Registrar of Co-operatives. Officers of the registrar also join the annual general meetings of co-operatives as auditors and as developmental partners to guide the members.

274. Regarding beneficial ownership information, the oversight and enforcement mechanism under the AML framework and supervisory activities discussed under section A.1.1 apply to co-operatives. The obligations concerning the identification and maintenance of beneficial ownership information on co-operatives by AML-obliged persons are supervised by the FIC and NAMFISA.

275. The FIC guidance note that was amended in 2025 contains new and more detailed guidance on the determination of beneficial ownership information of co-operatives. The authorities explained that the changes in the guidance note have already been integrated in their oversight and supervisory activities, however, since the changes are recent, their implementation could not be fully assessed during this review. Namibia is recommended to continue to monitor the implementation of recent changes in the guidance for identification of beneficial owners to ensure that adequate, accurate and up-to-date beneficial ownership information of all co-operatives is available in all cases.
Availability of information on co-operatives in EOIR practice
276. Namibia did not receive any requests for identity or beneficial ownership in relation to co-operatives during the review period, and peers have not reported any issues regarding the same.

A.2 Accounting records
Jurisdictions should ensure that reliable accounting records are kept for all relevant entities and arrangements.

277. The legal and regulatory framework contains sufficient obligations to maintain accounting records and underlying documentation by all relevant entities and arrangements in Namibia. These obligations are broadly set through a combination of company and tax laws. The Companies Act, Close Corporations Act, Trust Administration Act and Co-operatives Act contain obligations for the relevant entities and arrangements, while the Income Tax Act and the VAT Act contain obligations that apply to all legal entities and arrangements, including partnerships.
278. There are appropriate mechanisms to ensure that accounting records and underlying documentation are kept for at least five years, including when entities cease to exist.

279. Regarding the implementation of the legal and regulatory framework, the key supervisory functions are conducted by the Namibia Revenue Agency. These are complemented by the oversight role performed by the Public Accountants and Auditors Board and by the Registrar of Co-operatives.

280. Entities are required to submit accounting information through periodic tax returns. The Namibia Revenue Agency has carried out various monitoring, supervisory and enforcement activities to ensure compliance with these obligations. From 2023 to 2025, the rate of compliance with filing for income tax, for large taxpayers stood at an average of 85% while it was 47% for small and medium taxpayers. The rate of compliance for filing for VAT stood at an average of 96% for large taxpayers and 82% for small and medium taxpayers. When taxpayers fail to file their returns, the Namibia Revenue Agency conducts comprehensive risk-based examinations using third party information from sources such as local authority councils, ministries and other agencies such as the Financial Intelligence Centre, as well as financial institutions, to determine whether such non-compliant entities are involved in business activities. The entities conducting business activities are then selected for tax audits. From 2023 to 2025, the Namibia Revenue Agency conducted tax audits covering 12.4% of the total entities and additional tax assessments were raised.

281. Despite these supervisory efforts, there remains a concern regarding the percentage of entities (mainly small and medium taxpayers) that are not compliant with tax filing obligations. Namibia is recommended to strengthen the effectiveness of its supervisory and enforcement programmes to ensure that non-compliant entities do not affect the availability of accounting records.
282. Namibia received 20 requests for accounting information, and the requested information was provided in all cases.
283. The conclusions are as follows:
Legal and regulatory framework: In place
No material deficiencies have been identified in the legislation of Namibia in relation to the availability of accounting information.
Practical implementation of the standard: Largely Compliant

A.2.1 General requirements

284. The requirements to maintain accounting records and underlying documentation for all relevant entities and arrangements in line with the standard are set out through a combination of tax and company law obligations. The Companies Act (companies), CC Act (close corporations), TAA (trusts) and Co-operatives Act (co-operatives) contain record-keeping obligations for the relevant entities and arrangements. Further, the Income Tax Act (ITA), the VAT Act and the Customs and Excise Act impose similar obligations on companies, partnerships, trusts and co-operatives. The various legal regimes and their implementation in practice are analysed below.
Companies and close corporations

285. Every company, including a foreign company that establishes business in Namibia, must keep accounting records that adequately and fairly reflect its financial position and business activities (s. 292, Companies Act). The records must contain all entries of money received or expensed and a record of all goods or services sold. The records must enable the preparation of annual financial statements that conform with generally accepted accounting practice and must contain: i) a balance sheet and any notes or documents annexed to it; ii) an income statement and any notes attached to it; iii) a cashflow statement; iv) a directors' report; and v) an auditor's report.

286. The accounting records of the company may be kept at the company's registered office in Namibia or at a place outside of Namibia. Where the records are kept outside Namibia, they must be sent to a place in Namibia at intervals not exceeding 12 months. In the latter case, the records sent to Namibia must be complete and should enable the determination of a company's financial position. The records must also be available for inspection by the directors, external auditors and enable the preparation of the company's annual financial statements. The representative of auditors and accountants met during the on-site visit confirmed that in practice, they have always found all accounting records and underlying documentation (see paragraph 305) available at the company's premises in Namibia or easily accessed through online platforms. This position was also confirmed by NamRA's tax auditors. Consequently, the accounting records available in Namibia are sufficient to disclose with reasonable accuracy the financial position of the company at any time, including when such records are kept outside and submitted to a place in Namibia annually.

287. Copies of financial statements of public companies or private companies that are subsidiaries of public companies, must be submitted to BIPA, annually. Namibia has explained that the monitoring of the submission of such statements only started recently and there are no statistics that are readily available. Further, for all public companies that are listed, the financial statements of such companies are posted on the individual company websites.

288. Close corporations are also mandated to keep accounting records and prepare annual financial statements, as discussed in paragraph 285. In addition, the accounting records of a close corporation must contain the accounting relating to the contributions of members, loans disbursed and any other payments to members (s. 56, CC Act). Further, instead of an auditor's report, the financial statements of a close corporation contain a report of the corporation's accounting officer. $^{17}$ The accounting records of the close corporation must be kept at the corporation's registered office or business premises in Namibia.
289. If accounting records are not kept in bound books, the company or close corporation must take adequate measures to prevent falsification and to ensure that any falsification can be detected.
$^{17}$ Every close corporation is obliged to appoint an accounting officer who is a member of a professional body (such as accountants body) and cannot be one of the members of the close corporation
GLOBAL FORUM ON TRANSPARENCY AND EXCHANGE OF INFORMATION FOR TAX PURPOSES: NAMIBIA 2026 (SECOND ROUND) © OECD 2026
Trusts and co-operatives
290. The Trust Administration Act (TAA) and Co-operatives Act contain robust obligations that require the keeping of accounting records of trusts and co-operatives in line with the standard.

291. Section 20 of the TAA requires every trustee to maintain records of the trust property that identify the assets, liabilities, income and expenses relating to the property. In addition, the trustee must maintain all transactions and advisory services related to the trust accounts, including the trust investments. The trustee must also keep a record of all payments made to themselves or any other trustees. All these records must also be submitted to the MOHC, annually. The definition of a trustee as contained in the ITA covers both professional and non-professional trustees (see paragraph 240 and below).

292. Similarly, co-operatives are obliged to keep accounting records in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles that fairly reflect the situation, business, and explain the transactions and financial position of the co-operative (s. 63, Co-operatives Act). The co-operative is also mandated to prepare annual financial statements that contain a balance sheet, an income statement, the board's report and the auditors' report.

293. The financial statements of the co-operative must be audited by an external auditor and a copy of these audited statements must be submitted to the Registrar of Co-operative, annually (s. 64, Co-operatives Act).
Tax law requirements

294. Tax law requirements provide the primary source of obligations to ensure the availability of accounting records for partnerships and provide complementary obligations for companies, close corporations, trusts and co-operatives. There are no direct obligations in the ITA requiring taxpayers to maintain accounting records. However, taxpayers must maintain and provide records to NamRA to comply with certain obligations.

295. Firstly, all companies, close corporations, partnerships, trusts and co-operatives liable to income tax in Namibia are required to submit an annual return to NamRA. The tax returns must be supported by financial statements that are certified by an accountant registered with the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Namibia (s. 62a, ITA) or a similar body. The financial statements of a close corporation must be certified by its accounting officer who must be registered with the Namibian Institute of Professional Accountants. Any person who submits such financial statements, including the auditor, must submit a statement on the scope of the examination carried out, of the books of account and of the underlying documents from which those books were prepared, and a statement, to the extent determinable from such examination, on whether the entries in those books and documents accurately reflect the true nature of any transaction, receipt, accrual, payment or debit (s. 63, ITA).

296. Secondly, taxpayers are required to produce for examination any deeds, plans, instruments, books, accounts, trade lists, stock lists, or other documents that are necessary for the administration of the ITA. This requirement facilitates tax audits and inspections.

297. The VAT Act supplements the requirements of the ITA in requiring all VAT registered taxpayers to maintain proper accounting records. The VAT Act elaborates on the situations where the accounting records of an entity may be maintained at a place outside of Namibia. It states that if the records are kept outside of Namibia, such records must be maintained in a computerised system that is linked to a registered place of business in Namibia and hence must be accessible from Namibia (s. 48, VAT Act). This requirement of the VAT Act further ensures that the system in place allows timely availability of accounting records in all cases.

298. Moreover, section 112(1)(a) of the Customs and Excise Act requires persons conducting business in Namibia to maintain the books, accounts, documents or information relating to business transactions.

This requirement extends beyond persons who import or export goods into or from Namibia. This is because section 113 of the act requires any person who sells, offers for sale, deals in, removes, or has recorded in their books any imported, excisable, or fuel-levy goods, or whose documents contain references to such goods, to be able to provide accountability of customs duties that were paid in respect of such goods.

299. Therefore, for purposes of compliance with direct and indirect tax obligations and customs duties, entities and arrangements are obliged to maintain accounting records, in line with the standard.
Retention period and entities that ceased to exist

300. The Companies Act and Co-operatives Act do not contain explicit obligations on the retention of accounting records, although both acts require that such records should always be available for inspection. On the other hand, the CC Act prescribes to retain the accounting records of a close corporation for at least 15 years (Regulation 9, General Regulations). The accounting records that are submitted to BIPA and the Registrar of co-operatives are maintained indefinitely.

301. Tax law contains more explicit obligations to maintain records for at least five years. Section 65(1)(f) of the ITA requires taxpayers to keep their accounting records for at least five years from the date of last entry of such records, while section 48(5) of the VAT Act requires the records to be kept for at least five years after the elapse of the tax period to which the records relate. The obligations of the tax laws cover all entities and arrangements (such as partnerships). In addition, the accounting records submitted to NamRA as part of tax returns and through tax audits are kept indefinitely.

302. Additionally, the accounting records of companies and close corporations that cease to exist must be maintained by appointed custodians (former directors in case of a company) or liquidators (see paragraphs 69 to 73). The accounting records of a co-operative that ceases to exist are submitted to the Registrar of Co-operatives (see paragraph 272).

303. Regarding trusts, the TAA (s. 26) mandates trustees to retain the records of a trust for five years, or longer if required by the MOHC, after the trust arrangement is terminated. If there is more than one trustee, all the trustees must comply with the obligation to maintain the accounting records.

304. Namibian authorities explained that although they have not received any requests regarding entities that ceased to exist, they have accessed such information without any challenges, for domestic cases. In conclusion, the various obligations taken together ensure the retention of accounting records, including when the entities or arrangements cease to exist, in accordance with the standard.
A.2.2 Underlying documentation

305. Entities are required to keep accounting records that are sufficient to show and explain the transactions of the entity (s. 292, Companies Act, s. 56(1), CC Act and s. 63 (1), Co-operatives Act). These records must explain the entity's transactions and financial state and must include:
\- documents showing the company’s assets and liabilities
\- a fixed-asset register indicating the dates of acquisition, cost, depreciation (if applicable), dates and amounts of any revaluation, and the dates and proceeds of any disposals
\- day-to-day records detailing all cash received and paid out, with sufficient information to identify the purpose of each transaction

\- where the company deals in goods, records of all goods bought and sold. Except in ordinary retail trade, these records must identify the goods and the buyers and sellers with enough detail to determine their nature and identity
• annual stocktaking statements.
GLOBAL FORUM ON TRANSPARENCY AND EXCHANGE OF INFORMATION FOR TAX PURPOSES: NAMIBIA 2026 (SECOND ROUND) © OECD 2026

306. The ITA (s. 63(1)) further specifies that all taxpayers should maintain all books of accounts and the documents from which the books of accounts were drawn and the documents that support the true nature of any transaction, receipt accrual or payment. These comprehensive records would also cover underlying documentation. Moreover, the VAT Act (s. 48(1)) states that taxpayers should keep copies of all invoices, tax credit and debit notes, customs documentation relating to imports and exports and any other records the Commissioner may determine.

307. When entities cease to exist, or trust arrangements are terminated, the obligations discussed in paragraphs 301 to 303 also apply to ensure that the underlying documentation shall be maintained in line with the standard.
Oversight and enforcement of requirements to maintain accounting records

308. The obligations to maintain accounting records and underlying documentation are enforceable through a range of penalties that address various forms of non-compliance, including failures by legal entities or arrangements to keep proper records as required, non-submission of tax returns, and breaches of the rules governing the preparation of financial statements.

309. If a company fails to comply with the obligations to keep its accounting records and underlying documentation, every director or officer of the company responsible for that failure or who fails to rectify the non-compliance, is liable to a fine not exceeding NAD 8 000 (EUR 362) or to imprisonment for a period not exceeding two years or both (s. 292(4), Companies Act). The CC Act (s. 82) prescribes a similar offence for the members of a corporation that fail to keep proper accounting records and underlying documentation.

310. In addition, if a company fails to prepare annual financial statements, the directors and officers of the company are liable to a fine not exceeding NAD 2 000 (EUR 90.5) and imprisonment for a period not exceeding three months, or both. Moreover, if a company issues, circulates or publishes any financial statements that are materially incomplete or otherwise fail to meet the requirements of the act, every director or officer involved in such issuance is liable to a fine of up to NAD 1 000 (EUR 45), imprisonment for a period not exceeding three months, or both (s. 295, Companies Act). A similar penalty regarding close corporations exists.

311. The tax law obligations also carry sanctions for non-compliance. Section 66 of the ITA states that a taxpayer who fails to submit a tax return, omits information from a tax return, or makes an incorrect statement in the tax return, is subject to a fine equal to double the top-up tax. Moreover, the ITA contains criminal sanctions. A taxpayer who fails to file a tax return, or submits a false statement, is liable on conviction to NAD 300 (EUR 16) or imprisonment not exceeding three months or both (s. 65).

312. The VAT Act also prescribes relevant penalties. Failure to maintain proper accounting records attracts a penalty not exceeding NAD 8 000 (EUR 362) or imprisonment not exceeding two years, or both.

313. The Namibian authorities explained that in practice, the supervisory and enforcement measures related to the maintenance of accounting records and supporting documentation are typically carried out within a broader compliance monitoring and enforcement framework. These measures generally comprise a mix of preventive programmes, verification procedures and audits.
Supervision by the Namibia Revenue Agency

314. NamRA is the main supervisory agency conducting key oversight and enforcement to ensure compliance with accounting records keeping obligations. NamRA employs various mechanisms that include taxpayer education and service management to improve voluntary compliance. Further, taxpayer returns are examined for accuracy and where applicable, additional tax assessments are raised, or audits and investigations conducted.

text: 323. Between 2022 and 2025, NamRA conducted an average of 7 000 tax audits annually with a total of 24 832 (12.4% of entities) audits conducted overall. The audits evaluate the availability, completeness and accuracy of accounting records and underlying documentation kept by taxpayers. NamRA reported that in most cases, taxpayers kept accounting records, although there were instances of under-reported incomes and mismatches in the records. Where the taxpayers could not provide all the accounting records, additional assessments were raised and the taxpayers must submit the missing records.

324. In general, additional taxes amounting to over EUR 233 million were raised from all the tax audits conducted. During this period, Namibia was running a penalty waiver amnesty programme and as such, only principal taxes were payable. In addition, through these audits, NamRA identified 25 non-compliant taxpayers that were eventually assessed taxes amounting to NAD 123 292 936 (EUR 5 579 875).

325. The information submitted by the Namibian authorities indicates that NamRA has employed varied approaches to improve compliance, thereby ensuring that part of the accounting information is submitted to the authorities. They have supplemented this by carrying out tax audits and investigations to recover undeclared tax and consequently ensure that entities keep accounting records and underlying documents. However, there are concerns regarding non-compliant entities.

Inactive (non-compliant) entities

326. The statistics provided by Namibia demonstrate that an estimated 63% of the entities are not compliant regarding the obligation to file income tax returns to NamRA. The rate of non-compliance for VAT is much lower at 17%. Although NamRA does not have a formal categorisation for such entities, the Namibian authorities explained that most of the non-compliant entities are the same population that has been classified as inactive by BIPA as discussed in paragraphs 99 and 176 to 177. Most of the entities are close corporations that, in some cases, did not commence business operations, or entities that are classified as small taxpayers.

327. The authorities explained that the list of taxpayers who have not submitted their returns within the required timeframe (non-filers) is periodically extracted for further management. If a taxpayer does not respond to initial outreach, a demand letter is issued after 21 days. Should there still be no response, a second demand letter follows 14 days later. These steps are designed to give taxpayers multiple opportunities to file before stronger enforcement measures are considered.

328. When taxpayers fail to respond even after the demand letters, their cases are escalated for audit or investigation. At this stage, risk management, intelligence and regional teams all conduct various activities on a risk basis to identify non-filers that may be actively engaged in business activities. The risk management unit utilises data from tax filings to detect high-risk non-filers and identify patterns of non-compliance. The Intelligence unit collaborates with other agencies such as the FIC and BIPA to identify potential non-filers involved in high-risk sectors like mining. Lastly, NamRA teams and inspectors based in different regions conduct field visits to establish if the non-filers are engaged in business activities. They work closely with local councils that may have issued tenders to such entities. Where it is identified that the non-filers are engaged in business, audits are conducted.

329. Despite these coordinated efforts to manage non-filers and improve overall tax compliance, there is still an issue with non-compliant entities, especially regarding filing for income tax purposes. Notably, the rate of compliance with VAT returns is higher, implying that there are entities that are engaged in business and not complying with their obligations to file the annual income tax returns. Consequently, Namibia is recommended to strengthen its supervision and enforcement mechanisms to ensure that accounting records and underlying documentation are available for all relevant legal entities and arrangements in all cases.
Oversight by other agencies

330. An external auditor must audit the annual financial statements of companies and co-operatives. All registered audit firms and registered auditors or accountants accredited by the Public Accountants and Auditors Board undergo periodic quality assurance reviews, which assess both the firm's internal quality controls and the individual practitioner's adherence to auditing standards through audit file inspections. Review outcomes can be either satisfactory, indicating full compliance and resulting in the next quality assurance review being scheduled after three years, or unsatisfactory, meaning deficiencies were identified; in such cases, the firm or practitioner must implement improvements and undergo a re-review after one year.

331. The representatives of the Public Accountants and Auditors Board explained that, typically, auditors examine the accounting records of the entity, including detailed ledgers, reconciliations, and supporting schedules and underlying documents such as invoices, contracts, confirmations, or bank statements to form their professional opinions on the entity's accounts. They explained that in practice, auditors must be given access to all evidence necessary to obtain appropriate audit assurance.

332. Regarding co-operatives, the supervisory functions for accounting records maintenance are also supervised through audits conducted by officials from the office of the Registrar of co-operatives. In practice, approximately 99% of co-operatives are audited annually. These audits examine the completeness of the annual financial statements, supporting accounting records, minutes of meetings, and any other documentation required to demonstrate compliance. Officers from the Registrar's office also attend annual general meetings of co-operatives both in their capacity as auditors and as development partners, providing guidance and support to members.

A.3 Banking Information
Banking information and beneficial ownership information should be available for all account holders.

334. Namibia has in place a legal and regulatory framework that broadly requires banks to identify account holders and customers, including determining and maintaining identity information on beneficial owners of accounts and specific types of information on transactions, for a minimum period of seven years. The Bank of Namibia is responsible for the licensing, regulation and prudential supervision of banks, while the Financial Intelligence Centre is responsible for the oversight and enforcement of anti-money laundering obligations.
335. The legal and regulatory framework regarding the availability of beneficial ownership information on all bank accounts is in place, but some improvement is needed on retention of records.

336. Regarding the retention of banking information when a Namibian bank ceases to exist and/or operate, or a branch of a foreign bank ceases operating in Namibia, there are no clear obligations that the records of the bank, including transactional and customer identification information, be maintained for a minimum period of five years. Accordingly, Namibia is recommended to address these gaps.
337. Namibia received 19 requests for banking information, and the requested information was provided in all cases.

A.3.1 Record-keeping requirements

339. The Bank of Namibia is mandated to license, regulate and supervise all banks in Namibia. Banking law is mainly laid out through the Banking Institutions Act and is complemented by the Financial Intelligence Act (FIA), in regulating the operation of banks. There are seven commercial banks currently operating in Namibia.
Availability of banking information

340. The legal obligations on banks to maintain and report all transactional information on all account holders arise from the Banking Institutions Act, as well as from the AML framework. These are further complemented by commercial law, which requires banks to maintain their accounting records.

341. Section 59 of the Banking Institutions Act requires banks to keep core banking systems that contain records and documentation covering all functional areas and other records as are necessary to reflect the true and fair state of the affairs of the bank and explain the transactions and financial position of the bank.
GLOBAL FORUM ON TRANSPARENCY AND EXCHANGE OF INFORMATION FOR TAX PURPOSES: NAMIBIA 2026 (SECOND ROUND) © OECD 2026

342. Further, the bank is required to identify and maintain identity information, including CDD, on its clients and to maintain a record of all transactions carried out by or on behalf of each account holder (s. 21, FIA). The transactional records maintained pursuant to the AML framework should be sufficient to show the source and recipient of funds and to demonstrate an audit trail. Sections 26 and 27 of the FIA explain the transactional information that should be maintained by a bank, and it includes:
• the identity of the person conducting the transaction
\- the manner in which the identity of a person was established and CDD records
• the nature and date of the transaction
• all accounts at the bank that were involved in the transaction
• the amount involved and the parties to the transaction
\- client files and business correspondences
\- all sufficient records that enable the reconstruction of any transaction for both clients and non-clients, whether concluded as a single transaction or during a business relationship.
343. Based on these obligations, banks are expected to maintain all account opening documents and financial transactional information on all accounts in accordance with the standard.

344. Banks must keep the information on their customers and any transactions on their accounts for at least five years from the end of a business relationship, or if the business relationship is still ongoing, from the date of the transaction (s. 27(1), FIA). The transactional information maintained under the Banking Institutions Act must also be maintained for at least five years from the date of last entry (s. 59(2), Banking Institutions Act).

345. A bank in Namibia will cease to exist either by amalgamation through a merger, consolidation or transfer of its assets to another bank or through voluntary and involuntary winding up. When the bank ceases to exist because of an amalgamation, all its records, including CDD and beneficial ownership information, will be held by the surviving bank.

346. The Banking Institution Act details procedures of winding up and liquidation of a bank and places the responsibility to supervise the liquidation process of a bank, on the Bank of Namibia. The winding up and liquidation process applies to any bank licensed in Namibia, including a branch of a foreign bank operating in Namibia. Section 72 of the Banking Institutions Act indicates that for the winding up of the affairs of the bank, the Banking Institutions Act takes precedence over the provisions in the Companies Act. At the time of the on-site visit, one bank was undergoing liquidation, and it is not ascertained that all the records of that bank will be retained for at least five years as required by the standard. Namibian authorities explained that they are in the process of updating the Banking Institutions Act to incorporate a clear and explicit bank-specific post-cessation record-retention requirement, including in respect of foreign bank branches ceasing operations in Namibia. As it stands, the Banking Institutions Act does not contain provisions on the retention of the records of the bank after the bank ceases to exist and generally, the legal and regulatory framework does not contain any obligations to require the retention of the records of a bank that ceases to exist or otherwise ceases its operations. Therefore, Namibia is recommended to ensure that banking information is available for the minimum period of five years, in all cases after a bank ceases to exist or ceases its operations in Namibia.
Beneficial ownership information on account holders

347. The standard requires that beneficial ownership information be available in respect of all accounts. In Namibia, this requirement is implemented through the provisions of the FIA and binding guidelines contained in the FIC guidance note. This AML framework obliges banks to carry out CDD, identify and maintain beneficial ownership information on all account holders and on one-off transactions.
