348. The definition of beneficial owners contained in the FIA and the FIC guidance note, as discussed under section A.1, allows for the identification of beneficial owners of bank accounts held by any relevant entity or arrangement, in line with the standard.

349. As discussed in paragraphs 118 to 122, the FIC guidance on the identification of beneficial owners was amended in 2025, with more examples of how to conduct CDD in complex ownership structures having been added. The representatives of the banks interviewed during the on-site visit demonstrated a clear understanding of the concept of beneficial owner for each type of legal person and explained that the amendments to the guidance note merely highlighted aspects that are already elaborated in the FIA and are being practised. The Namibian authorities explained that the 2025 amendments were mainly targeted to improve the implementation of the obligations contained in the Companies Act and the CC Act. Nevertheless, since these amendments are recent and are also applicable to banks, Namibia should monitor the implementation of recent changes in the guidance for identification of beneficial owners to ensure that accurate, adequate and up-to-date beneficial ownership information on bank accounts is available in all cases (see Annex 1).

350. The AML framework provides extensive requirements for carrying out CDD. Banks are required to identify their customers, identify their beneficial owners and take reasonable measures to verify the identity of the beneficial owners before establishing a business relationship. If a bank cannot complete CDD measures, then it cannot commence a business relationship or complete a transaction. Moreover, if there is an already established and ongoing business relationship, the AML-obliged person must terminate the relationship and file a suspicious transaction report to the FIC (see paragraph 181).

351. Banks must conduct ongoing due diligence by keeping customer and beneficial ownership information up to date, monitoring transactions for consistency with a client's profile, and scrutinising complex or unusual activities. They must also apply enhanced due diligence for high-risk clients, suspicious transactions, or cases where previously collected identification data appears unreliable or raises concerns of money laundering or terrorism financing.

352. The AML framework allows banks to apply simplified CDD measures only where there is no suspicion of money laundering or terrorism financing. Even where simplified CDD is applied, the bank is still required to identify and verify the identity of all beneficial owners of the customer.

353. Regarding the updating of CDD and beneficial ownership information on existing clients, Guidance note no. 4 of 2009 on the Implementation of a Compliance Regime requires AML-obliged persons to review CDD at least once every year for high-risk clients and at least once in two years for all other clients. Further banks are required to implement internal policies that are consistent with the national or sectoral money laundering or terrorism financing risk assessments (s. 20A, FIA). The Namibian authorities explained that such internal policies should facilitate the updating of CDD and beneficial ownership information (see paragraph 187). The representatives of the banks met during the on-site visit explained that for most of them, their internal policies required the updating of CDD based on the trigger factors explained at paragraph 185, and at least once annually for high risk clients, at least once in three years for medium-risk clients and at least once in five years for low risk clients. The representatives further explained that this specified frequency may vary, especially regarding the medium and low risk categories, although in practice they have all set frequencies under five years. The authorities can sanction a bank for setting inappropriate policies. The Namibian authorities explained that they have reviewed all the policies of the seven banks and appropriate frequencies have been set (once annually for high risk, once in three years for medium risk and once in five years for low risk). Considering that banks may set frequencies in their internal policies that differ from those stated in the guidance, Namibia should align the provisions of the binding guidance and the practice by banks to ensure that CDD and beneficial ownership information are updated appropriately for all bank accounts (see Annex 1).

354. As explained in paragraphs 191 to 191, the FIA allows banks to rely on third parties or business introducers to conduct CDD; however, the ultimate responsibility and accountability for CDD remains with the bank. The measures put in place in the FIA, including the fact that the third party itself must be subject to AML regulation and the bank should be able to obtain full CDD documentation immediately from such a third party, are in line with the standard. Moreover, banks are not permitted to rely on third parties for CDD in cases of high-risk clients such as politically exposed persons, clients from high-risk jurisdictions or clients with complex ownership structures.
Oversight and enforcement

355. The Bank of Namibia is responsible for the licensing and prudential supervision of banks in Namibia while the FIC is mandated to supervise the implementation of AML obligations. In practice, the two public authorities collaborate closely on supervision, including in monitoring record keeping practices.

356. Both the Banking Institutions Act and the FIA contain administrative and criminal sanctions applicable to non-compliance. Any intentional action by a bank to mislead through the records it maintains is an offence which is sanctionable upon conviction, to a fine not exceeding NAD 2 million (EUR 90 154) or imprisonment not exceeding 10 years or both (s. 92 and 94, Banking Institutions Act). The sanctions contained in the FIA are elaborated in paragraphs 192 and 193.

357. Regarding the Bank of Namibia's prudential supervision, comprehensive and targeted inspections were conducted across banks. Reviews covered governance and other areas. A total of 1 full-scope and 12 targeted on-site inspections were conducted between 2022 and 2025. No risks were identified regarding the maintenance of transactional records.

358. Regarding AML obligations, the oversight and supervisory mechanism conducted by the FIC, as discussed in paragraphs 196 to 206, applies to banks. Utilising its annual compliance assessment and supervision methodology, the FIC conducts risk-based supervision to examine the implementation of AML obligations, including conducting CDD and identifying beneficial owners of bank account holders.

359. From 2022 to March 2026, the FIC conducted a mixture of on-site examinations, off-site examinations, thematic reviews and sectoral engagements. The thematic reviews are targeted and the majority of them were focused on how banks were implementing AML/CFT aspects such as financial sanctions screening. In 2025, the FIC started a new supervisory initiative termed “engagements with board of directors” as part of the new stakeholder engagement strategy where the FIC directly engages the board of directors of banks on AML/CFT compliance behaviour of the respective bank. This is meant to appraise those charged with governance of banks on AML/CFT compliance behaviour and matters, with a view that they will positively influence compliance from the top.

364. Sections B.1 and B.2 evaluate whether competent authorities have the power to obtain and provide information that is the subject of a request under an EOI arrangement from any person within their territorial jurisdiction who is in possession or control of such information, and whether rights and safeguards are compatible with effective EOI.
B.1 Competent authority's ability to obtain and provide information

Competent authorities should have the power to obtain and provide information that is the subject of a request under an exchange of information arrangement from any person within their territorial jurisdiction who is in possession or control of such information (irrespective of any legal obligation on such person to maintain the secrecy of the information).

365. The Namibian competent authority has broad access powers to obtain and provide information that is in possession or control of any person within the territorial jurisdiction of Namibia. The competent authority can access information from taxpayers and third-party information holders, including persons acting in a fiduciary capacity.

366. The powers to access information enable the competent authority to obtain information from the files and databases of the Namibia Revenue Agency and to issue notices to government agencies, banks, taxpayers and any other information holders. These access powers can be used regardless of domestic tax interest. In case of failure on the part of the information holder to provide the requested information, the competent authority has adequate powers to compel the production of information. Finally, secrecy provisions contained in Namibian law and practice are broadly compatible with the effective exchange of information.
367. Namibia has already applied these access powers to provide responses to treaty partners in 22 requests.

B.1.1 Ownership, identity and banking information
Accessing information generally

369. The Minister in charge of finance is Namibia's competent authority for the international exchange of information in application of EOI instruments. The Minister has delegated the operational role of the competent authority to the Commissioner of NamRA. Operationally, the role has been further delegated to the head of the EOI unit.
370. Section 64(1) of the ITA states that:

For the purpose of obtaining full information in respect of any income of any taxpayer or of any part thereof, the Minister may require any person to produce for examination by the Minister, or by any person appointed by him or her for that purpose, at such time and place as may be appointed by the Minister in that behalf, any deeds, plans, instruments, books, accounts, trade lists, stock lists or documents which the Minister may deem necessary for the purposes of this Act, and if any such deeds, plans, instruments, books, accounts, lists or documents are not in the English language the Minister may by notice in writing require the taxpayer to produce at his or her own expense and at such time and place as may be appointed, a translation in the English language prepared and certified by a sworn translator or a person other than a sworn translator approved by the Minister.

371. This power can be exercised in circumstances where information is held by any person acting in an agency or fiduciary capacity, including nominees and trustees. By its wording, the provision appears to indicate a limitation by referring to “income of any taxpayer”. However, the Namibian authorities explained that the power is interpreted as enabling the Commissioner to execute all his/her functions, including the function of reciprocal assistance to treaty partners that is enshrined in section 100 of the ITA and Article 32(3)(e) of the Namibian Constitution (see B.1.3). Therefore, the power has been used to access information for EOI purposes, regardless of whether the person subject to the request is a taxpayer in Namibia or whether the requested information is subject to income taxes.

372. NamRA can exercise this power without the need to open any form of tax audit or inquiry. However, where needed, such as in the case of non-compliance by an information holder, audits or investigations may be instituted (see paragraph 392). Further, Namibian authorities have confirmed that NamRA's powers to access information are not affected by the expiration of statutory record retention periods. NamRA would still exercise its access powers and request information. However, where the information holder no longer possesses the requested information because it was lawfully disposed of following the expiry of the retention period, the information holder cannot be sanctioned for failing to produce such information.

373. The powers conferred by this section are used for obtaining all types of information, including accounting information in respect of all relevant entities and arrangements in Namibia, regardless of whether they are taxable and registered with NamRA. Further, information held by any other public authorities is obtained using the same powers conferred by the ITA.

374. The EOI unit officials have direct access to NamRA databases and access them to obtain information that is already available within the tax administration, including tax returns, financial statements and other accounting information obtained through tax audits or submitted through VAT returns. If the requested information is not available within NamRA databases, the EOI unit officials directly issue notices to any other information holders using the powers contained in section 64(1) of the ITA.

375. Namibia has used its access powers to answer 22 EOI requests already. The main sources of information for EOI purposes were NamRA records and databases, and BIPA. In other cases, banks, audit firms, trustees and taxpayers were also used to obtain the requested information. There have been no difficulties in using the access powers.

Accessing beneficial ownership information
376. The competent authority can access beneficial ownership information from various sources: BIPA for companies and close corporations, or the MOHC for trusts.

377. Additionally, beneficial ownership information is available from AML-obliged persons, particularly banks. Section 44(1) of the FIA states that no duty of secrecy or confidentiality arising from any other law or from common law can impede the disclosure of information by AML-obliged persons to the authorities that include NamRA.

378. In practice, when the competent authority receives a request for beneficial ownership information about a company, it first consults the list of inactive entities published on the BIPA website (see paragraph 173). If the entity subject of the request does not appear on this list, the competent authority issues a notice to BIPA to obtain the beneficial ownership information. If the entity is listed as inactive, meaning it has not yet submitted its beneficial ownership information to BIPA, the competent authority instead collects the required information from AML-obliged persons, primarily banks (see paragraph 381). On average, the process of obtaining beneficial ownership information from public authorities takes about 7 days, and from banks about 14 days.
379. Namibia received 13 requests for beneficial ownership information and successfully provided the requested information evenly relying on BIPA, the MOHC and the banks.
Accessing banking information

380. There are no special procedures to obtain banking information, and the competent authority uses NamRA's routine administrative powers conferred under the ITA (see paragraph 370), to send notices to produce information to banks.

381. The Namibian authorities explained that they do not have specific requirements that a requesting jurisdiction must include in its request to enable the gathering of banking information. The information included should be sufficient to identify the bank account or the account holder. If the requesting jurisdiction has only identified the account holder and the bank account number is not provided, the competent authority will send notices to all banks to check for the banking information on the person subject to the request.

382. The notice requesting information from banks usually provides for two weeks within which the bank should submit the requested information. In practice, Namibian authorities have informed that the requested information is often received within this two-week period. However, if the requested information relates to old records, the time frames may differ. Namibia obtained and provided banking information in accordance with the standard in all the 19 requests received.
B.1.2 Accounting records

383. The powers described under section B.1.1 can be used to obtain accounting records from any information holder, including the taxpayers themselves. Requested accounting records are typically already available to NamRA through financial statement filings alongside tax returns. Where additional underlying documentation is required, it is obtained by the competent authority from tax auditors and taxpayers themselves.

384. Namibia received 20 EOI requests for accounting information and provided all the requested information. In all cases, multiple sources such as NamRA databases, company auditors and taxpayers were used.

B.1.3 Use of information gathering measures absent domestic tax interest

385. The legal and regulatory framework and Namibia's practice ensure that NamRA's access powers to gather information can be used to address any incoming EOI requests, without any requirement of domestic tax interest. Moreover, when exercising its access powers, NamRA does not have to justify to the holder of the information its interest in obtaining it. Section 100 of the ITA refers to agreements entered into with a view to reciprocal assistance in the administration of and the collection of taxes under the income tax laws of Namibia and the partner country $^{20}$ and provides that tax secrecy does not apply in these cases. The Namibian authorities consider this sufficient to use the access powers for EOI purposes, and this has never been challenged by any information holder.

386. The Namibian competent authority confirmed that for most of the requests received, there was no immediate domestic tax interest for Namibia, although in some cases, Namibia noted some elements of potential non-compliance with Namibian tax obligations and such cases were referred for tax audit.
B.1.4 Effective enforcement provisions to compel the production of information

387. The standard requires that the jurisdictions have effective enforcement provisions, including sanctions for non-compliance to be applicable, for example, upon refusal or failure to supply the requested information. Namibia has in place effective enforcement provisions to compel the production of information.
Applicable sanctions

388. Sanctions can be applied against any person who fails to provide information requested by the competent authority. Section 65(1) of the ITA states that any person who fails to provide the requested information is liable to a penalty not exceeding NAD 300 (EUR 13.6) or imprisonment not exceeding three months, or both, upon conviction. If the person still fails to provide the requested information, a fine of NAD 30 (EUR 1.4) for each day that the request remains outstanding may be imposed.

389. Additionally, section 96 of the ITA provides that giving a false answer, whether orally or in writing, to any request for information, or preparing, maintaining or authorising false records, constitutes an offence punishable by a fine of NAD 2 000 (EUR 90) or imprisonment for up to two years, or both, upon conviction.

390. When the above-mentioned offences are committed by a body corporate, every public officer $^{21}$ or director, manager, partner or person involved in management of the body corporate may be sanctioned, unless the person proves that the acts or omissions constituting the offence took place without their knowledge or connivance.
391. The monetary sanctions appear not to be dissuasive enough. However, they may be accompanied by imprisonment, which would be dissuasive.

392. Moreover, the competent authority has the option to apply administrative measures or to compel the production of the requested information. The competent authority may escalate the matter to the audit or investigations teams. In the context of an audit, auditors would obtain the requested information, and if applicable, a tax assessment would be raised (s. 68, ITA). The investigators have the option to use inspection, search and seizure powers (approved by the commissioner) to obtain the requested information where necessary (s. 64(3), ITA). Any person who obstructs or hinders an officer conducting an audit or search and seizure is liable to the same sanction as the one described in paragraph 388.
$^{20}$ Namibia interprets country to include all jurisdictions

$^{21}$ The ITA (s. 93) requires every entity or arrangement that carrying on business in Namibia or having an office in Namibia to appoint a public officer. The public officer must be an individual resident in Namibia who is responsible for the service of documents to the entity. Where no specific appointment is made, then the director or other senior manager assumes the role of public officer.

Implementation of sanctions in practice

393. Namibia has not used these sanctions and compulsory powers for EOI purposes. Nevertheless, the sanctions have been applied successfully within the context of domestic cases, and information holder provided information when sanctions were applied.

394. In most cases, the need to use the enforcement powers available to the competent authority did not arise in practice since the information was provided by the information holders in a timely manner. Although Namibia provided full responses to 59% of the received EOI requests after one year, the main contributing factors for the delays were not associated with failure to apply sanctions (see discussion under Element C.5).

395. However, in one case, the Namibian competent authority did not provide a copy of an income tax return of an individual director of a company, which was requested by a peer. That director was not complying with his own tax obligation in Namibia, and when requested to file his income tax return, he did not file it. The authorities explained that whereas the director responded to the notices sent by the competent authority to provide information on the relevant company, he has not provided that specific piece of information, nor has he filed the tax return with NamRA. At that point, no further action was undertaken. Namibia reported that the case has been forwarded for tax audit after the on-site visit.

396. Other detailed accounting information from the auditors of the entity which also explained the directors' earnings was obtained and shared with the requesting jurisdiction. The requesting jurisdiction reported that the obtained information was sufficient to conclude its tax inquiries. In this case, despite the information requested (tax return) not being available, Namibia exercised its access powers by contacting the director to obtain this information and obtained useful alternative information, that the peer found sufficient, in the context of its tax audit procedures. Therefore, Namibia carried out actions to mitigate the lack of availability of the information requested. Namibia has since referred the case for audit. The availability, access or exchange of ownership, accounting or banking information was not affected. Nonetheless, it remains the case that Namibia did not initially exercise its enforcement measures against the director when this was needed to make the information requested available, although the matter has since been referred to audit. Namibia has further updated its EOI manual to require competent authority officials to review cases of delay or non-compliance for potential sanctioning.
B.1.5 Secrecy provisions

397. The legal and regulatory framework in Namibia imposes secrecy obligations on banks and certain professionals. NamRA has sufficient powers to override these obligations in the case of banking information and beneficial ownership information held by lawyers.
Bank secrecy

398. Section 85 of the Banking Institutions Act establishes a strict duty of confidentiality over information held by banks. However, the act also provides exceptions when the information is required or authorised by another law, including tax legislation. This means that banks are legally obligated to disclose banking information in response to notices issued in application of section 64(1) of the ITA (see paragraph 370).

399. The obligation to provide banking information was clearly demonstrated by the representatives of banks met during the on-site visit. Besides, Namibia was able to respond to 19 requests for banking information received during the review period by utilising its access powers to obtain information from the banks. No challenges regarding access to banking information arose during the review period.

Professional secrecy

400. The Legal Practitioners Act governs the legal profession in Namibia. It does not explicitly define or provide a scope for legal professional privilege. Namibian authorities explained that the basis for legal privilege is derived from English common law and has been recognised by Namibian courts. The authorities further explained that the privilege extends to all information received by the legal practitioner apart from situations where exceptions apply.

401. There is an exception to the legal professional privilege contained in the FIA regarding AML obligations. Section 44(1) of the FIA states that no duty of secrecy or confidentiality arising from any other law or from common law can impede the disclosure of information by AML-obliged persons. The FIA further stipulates that the information provided to a legal practitioner to provide legal advice or for use in contemplated legal proceedings remains confidential. The aforementioned exceptions contained in the FIA are in line with the standard.

402. Although the FIA exception to legal professional privilege clarifies the intended scope of this privilege, the representatives of the legal practitioners met during the on-site visit appeared uncertain about how the exception contained in the FIA would apply in practice for EOIR and indicated that if requested, they may seek the consent of their clients before disclosing the information. The practitioners stated that if requested by the FIC, they would promptly respond.

403. Legal practitioners are not a common source of information for the competent authority in Namibia and as such there has not been a case in practice where NamRA sought information from legal practitioners for EOI purposes; however, in theory, legal practitioners may be a source of beneficial ownership information. Therefore, Namibia should clarify the access powers of the competent authority to all stakeholders to ensure that professional secrecy does not impede the access powers of the competent authority (see Annex 1).

404. There are no other secrecy provisions that would impede the Namibian authorities from exercising their powers to access information from any other professionals. During the review period, Namibia successfully obtained accounting information from the auditors.

B.2 Notification requirements, rights and safeguards
The rights and safeguards (e.g. notification, appeal rights) that apply to persons in the requested jurisdiction should be compatible with effective exchange of information.
B.2.1 Rights and safeguards should not unduly prevent or delay effective exchange of information
Notification
405. Namibia's legal and regulatory framework does not require NamRA to notify the persons subject of an EOI request, either before or after the information is sent to the requesting jurisdiction.

406. Moreover, when NamRA exercises its right to access information, it only quotes the legal reference as contained in the ITA, which is general in nature and does not make any reference to EOI. There is no further requirement for NamRA to inform the information holder of the purpose of its request. Therefore, the risk that the taxpayer be indirectly informed of the existence of the EOI request is limited.

407. Further, the FIA contains an anti-tipping off provision, where persons liable can be fined up to NAD 100 million (EUR 4.5 million) or imprisonment not exceeding 30 years or both (s. 46, FIA). There are no similar provisions in the tax or banking laws. Nevertheless, the representatives of the banks met during the on-site visit confirmed that they do not inform their clients when they receive notices to produce information from NamRA.
Appeal rights

408. In general, there are no appeal rights associated with information obtained by NamRA. Therefore, if the person subject to the request or any other information holder is asked to provide information, there is no provision available to such a person to appeal.

409. The ITA (s. 71 and 73) provides for appeals and objections by taxpayers to the extent that tax assessments have been issued. Therefore, if the requested information was obtained in the context of an audit, the taxpayer would have the option to appeal any tax assessment thereon. In such a case, the taxpayer or their representative would not have access to the EOI file or the EOI nature of any information generated from the audit. The Namibian authorities explained that such a taxpayer would not be made aware that any information was collected pursuant to an EOI request from another jurisdiction.

410. Peer input from the review does not indicate any cases where notification or any rights and safeguards that apply to a person in Namibia unduly prevented or delayed effective exchange of information.
411. The conclusions are as follows:
Legal and regulatory framework: In place
The rights and safeguards that apply to persons in Namibia are compatible with effective exchange of information.
Practical implementation of the standard: Compliant
The application of the rights and safeguards in Namibia is compatible with effective exchange of information.

412. Sections C.1 to C.5 evaluate the effectiveness of Namibia's network of EOI mechanisms – whether these EOI mechanisms provide for exchange of the right scope of information, cover all Namibia's relevant partners, whether there were adequate provisions to ensure the confidentiality of information received, whether Namibia's network of EOI mechanisms respects the rights and safeguards of taxpayers and whether Namibia can provide the information requested in an effective manner.
C.1 Exchange of information mechanisms
Exchange of information mechanisms should provide for effective exchange of information.

413. Namibia has an extensive EOI network covering 157 jurisdictions through the Multilateral Convention, 11 Double Taxation Conventions (DTCs) and the Southern African Development Community Agreement on Assistance in Tax Matters (SADC AATM). The Multilateral Convention was signed by Namibia on 29 September 2020 and entered into force on 1 April 2021 in Namibia. All of Namibia's DTCs are in force. On the other hand, the SADC AATM has been signed and ratified by Namibia but is not yet in force.

414. Most of Namibia's EOI relationships are based on the Multilateral Convention, except for six EOI relationships $^{22}$ that are only established through the SADC AATM. Further, all the jurisdictions with which Namibia has a DTC are covered by the Multilateral Convention. Thus, the bilateral DTCs are not analysed in this report. Both the Multilateral Convention and SADC AATM provide for EOI in line with the standard and accordingly, all of Namibia's EOI relationships are in line with the standard.
415. The implementation of these instruments, particularly the interpretation of the concept of foreseeable relevance, including for group requests, complies with the standard.
416. The conclusions are as follows:
Legal and regulatory framework: In place
No material deficiencies have been identified in the EOI mechanisms of Namibia.
Practical implementation of the standard: Compliant
No issues have been identified that would affect EOIR in practice.

C.1.1 Requirement of foreseeable relevance

417. The standard for exchange of information envisages exchange of information to the widest possible extent but does not allow speculative requests for information that have no apparent nexus to an open inquiry or investigation. Exchange of information mechanisms should allow for exchange of information on request where it is “foreseeably relevant” to the administration and enforcement of the domestic tax laws of the requesting jurisdiction.

418. The Multilateral Convention provides for the exchange of “foreseeably relevant” information. The EOI provision of the SADC AATM (Article 4) contains the term “may be relevant”. The usage of the terms “may be relevant” is sufficient, as referenced in the commentary to Article 26(1) of the Model Tax Convention, if the parties to the EOI instruments agree on a meaning similar as “foreseeably relevant”. Namibian authorities confirmed that they interpret the terms “necessary” and “may be relevant” as having the same scope as “foreseeably relevant”.
Clarifications and foreseeable relevance in practice

419. The EOI manual provides for various aspects to be verified by the EOI unit to validate an incoming request, including the foreseeable relevance of the requested information. The manual reproduces the criteria listed in Article 5(5) of the commentary to the Model Agreement on Exchange of Information on tax matters and indicates that the foreseeable relevance must be assessed based on those criteria.

420. These criteria for determining the foreseeable relevance of the request are part of the validation checklist that the EOI official handling a request must use to validate every incoming request. The checklist is validated by the head of the EOI unit (see paragraphs 511 and 509). The EOI officials demonstrated a good understanding of the interpretation of foreseeable relevance and indicated that their approach is to share the requested information to the widest extent possible.

421. The EOI manual provides for a period of 14 days from the receipt of the request to seek clarification, if necessary, from the requesting jurisdiction. During the period under review, Namibia did not request any clarification regarding the foreseeable relevance of a request, nor did it reject any request.
Group Requests

422. The EOI standard includes a reference to group requests in accordance with paragraph 5.2 of the Commentary to Article 26 of the OECD Model Tax Convention. The foreseeable relevance of a group request must be sufficiently demonstrated, and the information requested should help to determine compliance with tax obligations by taxpayers in the group.

423. Namibia's EOI agreements and domestic law do not contain language prohibiting group requests. The EOI manual defines group requests and explains how to consider their foreseeable relevance. The EOI unit officials demonstrated knowledge of the concept and stated that if they received a group request, they would be able to provide information in accordance with Article 26 of the OECD Model Tax Convention and its commentaries.
424. Namibia neither received nor sent any group requests during the review period.
C.1.2 Obligation to exchange information in respect of all persons

425. The standard requires that exchange of information apply in respect of all persons and should not be restricted by tax residence or tax type considerations. In this regard, Article 26(1) of the OECD Model Tax Convention states that “the exchange of information is not restricted by Article 1” which defines the scope of persons covered by the convention.
GLOBAL FORUM ON TRANSPARENCY AND EXCHANGE OF INFORMATION FOR TAX PURPOSES: NAMIBIA 2026 (SECOND ROUND) © OECD 2026

426. The Multilateral Convention allows for exchange of information in respect of all persons. The application of the SADC AATM is not restricted in respect of the persons subject to the assistance and broadly defines the term “person” as including individuals, companies and any other bodies of persons. Therefore, all of Namibia’s EOI relationships allow for exchange of information in respect of all persons, in line with the standard.
427. In practice, Namibia has not received an EOI request where the person concerned was not a resident in either Namibia or the requesting jurisdiction.
C.1.3 and C.1.4 Obligation to exchange all types of information and Absence of domestic tax interest

428. The standard requires that EOI mechanisms should not permit the requested jurisdiction to decline to supply information solely because the information is held by a financial institution, nominee or person acting in an agency or a fiduciary capacity or because it relates to ownership interests in a person. They must also allow for exchange of information without regard to whether the requested jurisdiction needs the information for its own tax purposes.

429. The Multilateral Convention and the SADC AATM contain provisions equivalent to paragraphs 4 and 5 of Article 26 of the OECD Model Tax Convention, which provide for the exchange of all types of information, including in cases where the requested jurisdiction does not need the information for its own tax purposes.

430. In practice, Namibia received 19 requests for banking information, and the fact that the information was held by a bank did not prevent it from being processed. In addition, Namibia accessed information held by persons acting in an agency or fiduciary capacity, such as auditors (in 12 cases) and trustees (in 3 cases). Moreover, although the requests received by Namibia often involve a taxpayer resident in Namibia, the exchanged information was not necessarily of immediate tax interest to Namibia. Finally, as indicated under the section B.1 (paragraph 371), Namibia's domestic legislation provides for the possibility of exercising the competent authority's access powers to obtain information for reciprocal assistance to its treaty partners.
C.1.5 and C.1.6 Exchange of information for civil and criminal tax matters and unnecessity of dual criminality

431. The standard requires that exchange of information mechanisms provide for exchange of information in both civil and criminal tax matters and should not apply dual criminality principles to restrict exchange of information.
432. The Multilateral Convention and the SADC AATM permit the exchange of information in both administrative (or civil) and criminal tax matters.

433. Further, the Multilateral Convention, the SADC AATM and Namibia's domestic legal framework do not provide for the principle of dual criminality as a condition for answering an EOI request in criminal tax matters. Namibia therefore interprets these instruments and its legislation as providing for an exchange of information, including in cases where the facts under investigation would not constitute a criminal offence under Namibian law if it had occurred in Namibia.

434. In practice, Namibia did not receive any request in relation to criminal tax matters, but it indicated that it would exchange information with its partners regardless of the nature of the case in the requesting jurisdiction.

C.1.7 Provision of information in specific form requested

435. There is no restriction in Namibia's EOI instruments or in its legislation that would prevent it from providing the information requested in the form requested and specified by the requesting jurisdiction. In practice, Namibia and its peers have not encountered any difficulties regarding the form of the information exchanged, but no specific form was requested during the review period.
C.1. 8 and C.1.9 Signed agreements should be in force and be given effect through domestic law

436. The standard requires that jurisdictions take all steps necessary to bring into force signed EOI agreements expeditiously. In addition, for information exchange to be effective, the parties to an exchange of information arrangement may need to enact any legislation necessary to comply with the terms of the arrangement.

437. In Namibia, the Cabinet must grant approval for the ratification of a signed agreement. Following Cabinet approval, the agreement is submitted to the National Assembly for ratification, after which the instrument is formally incorporated into domestic law and subsequently proclaimed. The last DTC was signed in 2004 and entered into force 15 months later.

438. All of Namibia's bilateral treaties (Double Tax Conventions), the SADC AATM and the Multilateral Convention, have been ratified by Namibia. The SADC AATM has been signed and ratified by Namibia but is not yet in force because Article 15(2) of the SADC AATM provides that it will enter into force after two thirds of the member states have submitted their instruments of ratification to the Executive Secretary, and this quota has not yet been reached. The Multilateral Convention entered into force in Namibia on 1 April 2021, six months only after its signature.
439. Namibia has in place the legal and regulatory framework to give effect to its EOI mechanisms. No issues arose in practice.

C.2 Exchange of information mechanisms with all relevant partners
The jurisdiction's network of information exchange should cover all relevant partners, meaning those jurisdictions who are interested in entering into an information exchange arrangement.
440. Namibia currently has a wide EOI network covering 157 jurisdictions, owing to the Multilateral Convention. This network covers Namibia's main trade partners.

441. No Global Forum members indicated, in the preparation of this report, that Namibia refused to negotiate or sign an EOI instrument. One Global Forum member indicated that it approached Namibia to negotiate a DTC in 2010 but did not receive feedback on the same. The Namibian authorities explained that at that time, the government in Namibia had taken a decision not to enter into any negotiations for DTCs. That moratorium was lifted in 2024. Both Namibia and the member are parties to the SADC AATM and have both ratified it although the agreement is not yet in force (see Annex 2). Since the request from the Global Forum member was in the context of a DTC and not specifically an EOI instrument, and since both jurisdictions are already party to the SADC AATM, the absence of response from Namibia for the negotiation of a DTC is not considered as a material issue concerning this review.

442. More broadly, as the standard ultimately requires that jurisdictions establish an EOI relationship up to the standard with all partners who are interested in entering into such a relationship, Namibia confirmed that it would conclude EOI agreements with any new relevant partner who would so require.
443. The conclusions are as follows:
Legal and regulatory framework: In place
The network of information exchange mechanisms of Namibia covers all relevant partners.
Practical implementation of the standard: Compliant
The network of information exchange mechanisms of Namibia covers all relevant partners.
C.3 Confidentiality
The jurisdiction's information exchange mechanisms should have adequate provisions to ensure the confidentiality of information received.

444. The EOI agreements to which Namibia is a party contain confidentiality rules that are in line with the standard. Additionally, Namibian domestic legislation broadly provides for the confidentiality of tax information, including treaty-exchanged information, and the provisions apply to tax officials as well as any third-party contractors involved in handling taxpayer information. However, under the domestic legal framework, there is a possibility that information received through EOI could, in certain situations, be disclosed to persons not authorised under the applicable EOI agreements.

445. In practice, Namibia has extensive policies and measures in place to ensure the confidentiality of all exchanged information. The Namibia Revenue Agency has an active information security management team and comprehensive practices for physical and digital security to ensure confidentiality. All EOI unit staff are well-trained, experienced and aware of the aspects of confidentiality in their daily work.

EOI requests are clearly marked as treaty protected and confidential. All exchanged information, including background documents like correspondence with other competent authorities, is treated as confidential.
446. Namibia has not experienced any breaches of confidentiality with respect to exchanged information. Further, peers have not raised any concerns regarding confidentiality of exchanged information.

text: Practical implementation of the standard: Largely Compliant

No issues have been identified in the implementation of the existing legal framework on the confidentiality of information. However, once the recommendations on the legal framework are addressed, Namibia should ensure that they are applied and enforced in practice.
C.3.1 Information received: disclosure, use and safeguards

448. The Multilateral Convention and the SADC AATM ensure the confidentiality of information exchanged, in line with the standard. They require that the information obtained be kept secret under the same conditions as those provided for information obtained in application of Namibia's domestic legislation and is only communicated to persons or authorities concerned with the assessment or collection of taxes as well as procedures and prosecutions relating to taxes.

449. Regarding Namibia's domestic legal framework, the ITA contains provisions that ensure confidentiality of all information held by the tax administration, including information received under an EOI agreement, that comes to knowledge of any person. Section 4(1) of the act obliges every person carrying out the provisions of the act, to keep information secret. Additionally, the ITA requires such a person to take an oath of secrecy before any form of employment is commenced. The ITA creates sanctions for any breaches. A person who discloses tax information in breach of the law is liable, on conviction, to imprisonment for a period not exceeding two years (s. 4(3), ITA). The obligation is nonetheless lifted to allow for exchange of information with partners pursuant to an EOI agreement (s. 100, ITA).

450. In addition, section 35(1) of the Namibia Revenue Agency Act (NamRA Act) obliges any person employed by NamRA not to disclose tax information. Any person who violates these confidentiality obligations is liable, upon conviction, to a penalty of up to NAD 50 000 (EUR 2 262.9) or imprisonment for a period not exceeding five years, or both (s. 35(2), NamRA Act). Disciplinary sanctions such as loss of employment may also be applied in case of a breach. The Namibian authorities confirmed that the provisions of the ITA and NamRA Act apply to officials and third-party contractors and that the obligations continue to apply indefinitely after the employment or services contract ceases.

451. Exceptions to confidentiality contained in the NamRA Act may be broader than what is envisaged under Namibia's EOI agreements. The act provides an exception where a person employed by NamRA may disclose tax information if such disclosure is required for performing the person's duties under any other law or is required by order of a court of law (s. 35(1)(a) and (b)). Moreover, as discussed in paragraph 20, EOI agreements are at par with domestic statutes and as such, the provisions of Namibia's EOI agreements do not supersede provisions contained in domestic law. In practice, no situations arose and the risk of inappropriate disclosure is mitigated by the confidentiality label placed on all exchanged information which clearly states that the disclosure of that information is governed by the provisions of the relevant international agreement (see paragraph 463). Nevertheless, the disclosures authorised by the legal framework may lead to situations where treaty-exchanged information is disclosed beyond what is envisaged under the standard. Consequently, Namibia is recommended to ensure that the disclosure of information received pursuant to its exchange of information agreements is consistent with the standard.

452. The Terms of Reference, as amended in 2016, clarified that although it remains the rule that information exchanged cannot be used for purposes other than tax purposes, an exception applies where the EOI agreement provides that the information may be used for such other purposes under the laws of both contracting parties and the competent authority supplying the information authorises the use of information for purposes other than tax purposes. In the period under review, Namibia reported that there were no requests where the requesting partner sought Namibia's consent to utilise the information for non-tax purposes and similarly Namibia did not request its partners to use information received for non-tax purposes, since such use was not envisaged. The authorities confirmed that if asked, Namibia would grant the authorisation to use the exchanged information for non-tax purposes, provided the scope for such use is clearly and fully explained.
C.3.2 Confidentiality of other information

453. The confidentiality provisions in Namibia's EOI agreements and its domestic legal framework do not draw a distinction between information received in response to requests or information forming part of the requests themselves. As such, these provisions apply equally to all requests for such information, background documents to such requests, and any other document reflecting such information, including communications between the requesting and requested jurisdictions and communications within the tax authorities of either jurisdiction.

454. The EOI unit is the sole repository of all correspondence with other competent authorities. It does not share the request letter outside of the unit for the collection of information. Where information needs to be collected with the help of other NamRA officials (i.e. where the EOI unit does not have access to records, such as a document that is part of an audit file), a notice listing the required information is sent to the relevant officials. In any case, all these are tax departments, and their officials are bound by the confidentiality provisions.

455. The notice for collecting information from taxpayers and third-party information holders contains only minimal information. It states the legal basis (see paragraph 406), the requested information and the timeline within which the information should be provided. Where information is collected as part of a tax audit or tax investigation, it is not revealed that the audit or investigation is carried out based on an EOI request.

456. Moreover, the Namibian authorities have indicated that audit files do not contain a copy of the EOI request letter or competent authority correspondences, and that a taxpayer would not be able to access such information when appealing the decision following a tax audit.
Confidentiality in practice

457. Namibia has established comprehensive measures and policies to safeguard the confidentiality of all information obtained through its domestic tax administration processes and EOI mechanisms. These safeguards cover key areas, including human resource controls, physical security arrangements, and Information and Communications Technology (ICT) security systems, ensuring that information is protected throughout its lifecycle.
GLOBAL FORUM ON TRANSPARENCY AND EXCHANGE OF INFORMATION FOR TAX PURPOSES: NAMIBIA 2026 (SECOND ROUND) © OECD 2026
Human resources and training

458. All officials employed by NamRA undergo a pre-vetting process before employment, and it is only after a favourable outcome that a person will be offered employment. Additionally, vetting is conducted at any point during the employee's tenure to continuously assess the employee's suitability to handle taxpayer information. For third-party contractors, the contracting firms are obliged to vet their employees.

459. The requirement to maintain secrecy is also expressly incorporated into employment contracts and extends equally to permanent employees and contract staff. Further, all employees must complete and sign an Oath of Secrecy form which explicitly outlines confidentiality obligations. For third-party contractors, the requirement to ensure confidentiality is expressed through a service level agreement that contains confidentiality and non-disclosure clauses. Development partners offering capacity building technical assistance and who are likely to encounter taxpayer information must also sign the oath of secrecy form. All contractual agreements outline the legal consequences in case of breaching confidentiality.

460. NamRA enhances its confidentiality safeguards through structured and continuous staff training. Newly recruited employees receive induction training that includes guidance on confidentiality obligations, while all staff participate in annual awareness sessions on NamRA's Ethics and Integrity Policy. These sessions include dedicated modules on confidentiality and secrecy requirements. The training programmes apply to all NamRA employees, ensuring a consistent understanding and reinforcement of confidentiality standards across the organisation. At appropriate intervals, staff are continuously sensitised about cybersecurity awareness, ensuring they remain informed of emerging threats and security best practices.

461. Regarding staff departure policies, NamRA has established a structured offboarding process to ensure the timely removal of access rights for departing or transferring employees. The human resources department initiates this process by notifying all relevant business units of an employee's exit or internal transfer. In the event of cessation of employment with NamRA, NamRA's department of internal affairs immediately terminates the individual's physical access to NamRA premises, while the ICT department revokes access to all applicable systems. If the departing official was transferring out of the EOI unit, access to the EOI generic email account and all EOI related shared folders and physical access to the EOI office are all immediately withdrawn, ensuring that only authorised personnel retain access to sensitive information.
Physical and digital security measures

462. NamRA has implemented multiple physical security layers to safeguard confidential information maintained in physical form. Access to any office is restricted through an automated access control system, permitting entry only to authorised personnel, with access logs regularly reviewed to ensure accountability and detect irregularities. For the EOI office, only EOI officials have access using fingerprints and keys. Visitors and contractors are received at the front desk by their designated hosts, and their movements are continuously monitored throughout their presence on the premises. NamRA offices are further monitored through closed circuit television and protected by interior and exterior intrusion detection systems. The building is further monitored by security personnel posted on every floor.

463. Within the EOI office, information is managed in both paper and electronic form, although most of the information is in electronic form. Regarding paper information, the EOI office maintains a clean desk policy and uses lockable desk drawers and cabinets and a safe to store physical documents. The EOI office has its own printer and paper shredder. To prevent visual observation from outside the office, all windows have been fitted with frosted glass, enhancing privacy and reducing the likelihood of inadvertent disclosure of EOI information. Further, all paper copies of information are stamped with the markings “confidential – this information is provided under the provisions of an international tax agreement. Its use and disclosure are governed by the provisions of such tax agreement”. The same confidentiality markings are applied to information when it is received and processed in digital form.
GLOBAL FORUM ON TRANSPARENCY AND EXCHANGE OF INFORMATION FOR TAX PURPOSES: NAMIBIA 2026 (SECOND ROUND) © OECD 2026

464. Access to NamRA's ICT systems is managed through role-based access controls that give staff access based on their job roles. An active password policy ensures that staff use strong passwords, that must be changed regularly. The IT systems are continuously monitored for potential intrusion, while staff activity logs are kept and monitored.

465. Electronic information is protected through encryption, whether it is stored or in the process of being shared. The tools used to secure this information are themselves managed with strict controls, ensuring they are created, stored and updated in a secure manner. All electronic systems are regularly updated to address new risks and vulnerabilities, and safeguards are deployed to detect and block harmful software or suspicious activity.

466. EOI staff can only use official laptop computers to access their working files and folders. All media ports on these computers are blocked. Further, staff may access official emails using their personal mobile devices if they are registered with the ICT department, and access to the email server is monitored. Additional security measures include that the email application does not allow screenshots to be taken.
467. Taken together, the physical and digital security safeguards implemented by NamRA ensure that all taxpayer information remains protected.

468. NamRA's information security policy includes specific provisions governing the proper disposal of confidential information. There is no formal retention period for tax records maintained by NamRA and in practice most records are kept indefinitely. However, in case where records need to be disposed of, it is done in accordance with national record-management and disposal rules. Paper records are shredded and destroyed in a manner to prevent their reconstitution, while electronic devices that are due for decommissioning undergo a destruction protocol involving formatting and destruction of storage media.
Breach monitoring and breach response

469. In addition to the information security policy, policies on whistleblowing, security incident and internal investigation procedures, ethics and integrity, all contain procedures for monitoring confidentiality practices and detection of breaches. In practice, periodic security inspections and security risk assessments are conducted to identify vulnerabilities and ensure continuous improvement of physical and digital security controls.

470. When a breach is identified, the matter is formally submitted to NamRA's internal affairs and security department, which is mandated to conduct investigations pertaining to staff misconduct. If the breach consists of electronic information, the ICT department provides technical support to the investigation. Once the investigations are concluded, a report is submitted to the Commissioner with recommendations for disciplinary action, mitigation and preventive measures.

471. Namibian authorities reported that there have been no instances of breach of confidentiality regarding EOI information. In the last three years, there were two cases that involved confidentiality breaches on domestic tax information. The staff concerned lost their employment at NamRA.

472. The competent authority officials and other tax administration and government officials met during the on-site visit were well informed of their obligations regarding keeping information confidential. Namibia confirmed that any breach on the confidentiality of EOI information would be reported immediately to the Global Forum Secretariat and the relevant peers would be notified.

C.4 Rights and safeguards of taxpayers and third parties
The information exchange mechanisms should respect the rights and safeguards of taxpayers and third parties.
C.4.1 Exceptions to the requirement to provide information

473. The Multilateral Convention, the SADC AATM and all of Namibia's DTCs ensure that the contracting parties are not obliged to provide information which would disclose any trade, business, industrial, commercial or professional secret, information which is subject to attorney-client privilege, or information the disclosure of which would be contrary to public policy.

474. The EOI instruments do not define professional secrecy, and as described in section B.1.5 above, legal professional secrecy is derived from English common law. Despite the appropriate scoping and exceptions contained in the Financial Intelligence Act, the lack of certainty by legal practitioners in practice, on how they would handle a request from the competent authority to provide information, could delay the effective exchange of information. Namibia should clarify the access powers of the competent authority to all stakeholders to ensure that professional secrecy does not impede the access powers of the competent authority (see Annex 1).

475. In practice, Namibia has not experienced any practical difficulties in responding to EOI requests because of professional privilege. There were no cases during the review period where Namibia sought to obtain information pursuant to an EOI request from an attorney or similar professional, and peers did not raise any concerns pertaining to this aspect.
476. The conclusions are as follows:
Legal and regulatory framework: In place
No material deficiencies have been identified in the information exchange mechanisms of Namibia in respect of the rights and safeguards of taxpayers and third parties.
Practical implementation of the standard: Compliant
No material deficiencies have been identified in respect of the rights and safeguards of taxpayers and third parties.

C.5 Requesting and providing information in an effective manner
The jurisdiction should request and provide information under its network of agreements in an effective manner.

477. Having joined the Global Forum in 2019, Namibia's EOI unit was established in April 2021, and Namibia received its first EOI requests in December 2022. The annual volume of received requests is gradually rising. In total, Namibia received 22 EOI requests during the review period (1 April 2022 to 31 March 2025).

478. Namibia's EOI unit became fully operational with four dedicated staff that were deployed between September 2022 and February 2023 and is now well resourced. The EOI officials receive regular training, and the EOI manual has been updated to provide more guidance to officials.

479. At the beginning of the period under review, there was a limited understanding among the EOI unit officials on how to efficiently collect the requested information and respond to EOI requests. This initially affected Namibia's ability to provide the requested information to its peers in a timely manner. Whereas complete information was not provided in a timely manner, Namibia adopted an approach to provide multiple partial responses to the requesting jurisdiction(s) that were helpful for the jurisdictions to progress their tax audits. Further, Namibia has made changes in its operations of the competent authority office by training staff and documenting robust operational processes. The results of these are reflected towards the end of the review period, where considerable progress has been registered. Namibia should continue to monitor these new changes to ensure that the requested information is provided in a timely manner.

text: C.5.1 Timeliness of responses to requests for information

481. Namibia received 22 requests for information during the review period (1 April 2022 to 31 March 2025). The requests were primarily in respect of companies and trusts, with some requests on individuals where the individuals' ownership and management interests in companies and trusts were sought. Namibia also received two bulk requests for residency of individuals. During the review period, Namibia's main EOI partners were South Africa and Germany.

text: 483. Whereas the timeliness of responses was low at the beginning of the review period, it has gradually improved. The analysis of the effectiveness of exchange by Namibia takes into account several factors: the reasons for the long response times, the uniqueness of the two requests received in 2022 and still pending, and a developing culture of exchange. The analysis starts with the general situation before turning to the uniqueness of the 2022 requests.
Improving timeliness

484. Namibia fully answered 5% of the requests within 90 days and 32% within 180 days. Most of the requests (59%) were fully answered after one year. Namibia did not fail to respond to any valid EOI request, nor were any requests withdrawn by the requesting jurisdictions.

485. The Namibian authorities explained that ownership and banking information are often obtained in a short time frame. Similarly, where accounting information is readily available in the NamRA tax databases, it is obtained quickly.
486. For the requests received from 2023 to 2025, whereas the timeliness of responses was poor at the beginning of the review period, it has gradually improved.
GLOBAL FORUM ON TRANSPARENCY AND EXCHANGE OF INFORMATION FOR TAX PURPOSES: NAMIBIA 2026 (SECOND ROUND) © OECD 2026

487. The two reasons for the state of the timelines in responding to EOI requests received in 2023 and 2024 are the unique circumstances associated with some of the requests received by Namibia and the limited understanding within the competent authority officials, on the practice of EOI.

488. Firstly, most of the information that was provided after one year related to the underlying documentation as part of the requested accounting information. The Namibian authorities explained that most of the requests received in 2023 and 2024 concerned a similar group of taxpayers. From the description of the requests provided by the requesting jurisdiction and Namibian tax records, the taxpayers subject to the requests were non-compliant with tax filing obligations. Consequently, the competent authority anticipated a lack of cooperation of the non-compliant taxpayers and first sought to obtain the requested underlying documents from the external auditors of the persons' subject to the request. Some of the requested information, such as minutes of board meetings, could only be obtained from the persons themselves. The competent authority eventually obtained the information from the persons subject to the request. Additionally, some requests sought financial statements of tax years that were not yet ended as per the Namibian tax year (1 April to 31 March). In these, Namibia could only share the relevant financial statements once they were prepared as per Namibian reporting periods.

489. In contrast, all requests received between 1 January and 31 March 2025 were fully responded to within 180 days. The Namibian authorities explained that the requested information was obtained from tax databases, BIPA, banks and taxpayers themselves. While some of the requests received in 2025 had some of the characteristics of the previous requests, the response times demonstrate that the competent authority officials have improved on their efficiency.

490. Secondly, until late 2023, the Namibian competent authority was not aware that partial responses could be sent to requesting jurisdictions. The initial approach of the competent authority was to first collect all the requested information and provide complete responses, once all the information had been collected. The competent authority has since changed its approach and provided 50 partial responses to requesting peers.
Partial responses

491. In 2023, Namibia started providing the requested information in a partial manner. This approach enabled the competent authority to share the information that was already available within the NamRA databases, at BIPA and from banks as it continued to gather underlying accounting documentation from persons subject to the requests. In total, 50 partial responses (on 14 requests) were sent to the requesting jurisdiction(s).

494. From 1 January to 31 March 2025, all requests received were fully responded to within 180 days, so no partial information was shared.

495. Namibia has made progress to improve the timeliness and efficiency of its responses. At the beginning of the review period, it appears that there was limited understanding within the competent authority officials on how to efficiently collect the requested information and respond to EOI requests. This gradually improved and Namibia registered improvements, especially in 2025. Nevertheless, the progress made by Namibia is recent and accordingly, Namibia is recommended to continue monitoring the improved operations of the competent authority office to ensure that requested information is provided in a timely manner in line with the standard.
Pending cases

496. In December 2022, Namibia received two bulk requests that required Namibia to provide proof of tax residency on 6 939 individuals. The requests pertained to a bill on various matters of the financial markets including retirement funds in Namibia that was not yet passed into law. Namibia agreed with the requesting jurisdiction to put the requests on hold until 2023, in anticipation that the bill would have been passed into law by then. $^{23}$

497. In the meantime, Namibia started holding discussions with the information holders to determine how to fully identify the subject persons since the requests did not fully and adequately identify all persons in all cases. In March 2024, Namibia sent a request for clarification to the requesting jurisdiction, based on the discussions held with information holders. The requesting jurisdiction has not reported any challenges regarding the clarifications and reported they have held regular discussions with Namibia. Eventually, Namibia sent the first partial response in April 2025.

498. The Namibian authorities explained that the progress in confirming the tax residence of the individuals has been slow for various reasons. Some of the identity numbers provided by the requesting jurisdiction relate to old pre-independence identification cards while the persons concerned have since obtained Namibian national identity. In other cases, the identity numbers and tax registration numbers provided in the request do not match the tax registration records in Namibia. To date, Namibia has provided the confirmation of residence on 13% of the individuals. The peer confirmed that Namibia has provided regular updates on the status of these requests.
Status updates and communication with partners

499. Namibia's EOI manual directs that where the requested information cannot be provided within 90 days, status updates should be sent to the requesting jurisdiction(s). The manual differentiates two scenarios. First, where partial information has been gathered by the 90-day mark, a partial response is provided explaining the status of the request and providing an estimated timeline when the rest of the information shall be provided. Second, where no information has been collected yet, the status update should also be sent.

500. During the review period, Namibia mainly provided status updates as part of the partial responses sent to peers. Although no status updates were sent in 2025, this situation is acceptable in respect of the standard as the complete information was immediately sent after the lapse of 90 days. Further, although

Namibia did not send status updates at the initial 90-day mark for the requests received in 2022 and 2023, partial responses also serving as status updates were regularly sent thereafter (see paragraph 491).

501. Namibia reported that it has implemented a range of measures to establish and maintain effective communication channels with its peers. Peers did not report any difficulties in their communication with Namibia. The competent authority holds regular meetings with one of Namibia's main peers.

502. Further, Namibia reported that they have started requesting feedback on the information sent to requesting jurisdictions, and in one case, the requesting jurisdiction confirmed the usefulness of the received information.
C.5.2 Organisational processes and resources
Organisation of the competent authority

503. The Minister of Finance is designated as the competent authority under all of Namibia's EOI instruments. The Minister has delegated the competent authority role to the Commissioner, NamRA. For operational purposes, the role has further been delegated to the head of the EOI unit.
Resources and training

504. Namibia's EOI unit was established in April 2021 and was gradually staffed from September 2022 to February 2023, to reach three full-time officials who support the head of the unit. At full capacity, the unit should be staffed by six full time officials and a recruitment process is planned to fill the remaining positions.

505. The EOI unit is well-resourced and has appropriate organisational processes to support effective EOI. An EOI manual and Standard Operating Procedures set out procedures for handling incoming and outgoing requests, including the roles of both EOI staff and relevant tax offices. Since 2022, the EOI unit was relying on the Global Forum model manual on EOI and by November 2025, they customised out a NamRA version that is being implemented pending final administrative procedures. The model manual was being used to provide relevant guidance to NamRA officials, despite the delay in formal customisation.

506. An Excel-based tracking tool is utilised to keep track of all EOI requests, relevant timelines and status of responses. Moreover, the timely processing of requests forms part of the officials' annual performance agreements, with key performance indicators specifically linked to the prompt handling and completion of requests.

507. During the review period, the EOI unit officials have participated in various trainings organised by the Global Forum and other regional and international bodies. In addition, the EOI officials have trained other tax officials from the tax audit, investigations and other relevant NamRA departments.
Incoming requests
508. Namibia has detailed processes for receiving, handling and responding to incoming requests. The procedure is detailed in the EOI manual.
Competent authority's handling of the request

509. EOI requests can be received through the EOI generic email or through a courier. The officer who receives the request must immediately log the request into the tracking tool and complete all relevant fields. A case reference number must then be allocated. Once done, the officer informs the head of the EOI unit, who proceeds to allocate the request to one of the three specialist EOI officials. This process must be completed within three days.
GLOBAL FORUM ON TRANSPARENCY AND EXCHANGE OF INFORMATION FOR TAX PURPOSES: NAMIBIA 2026 (SECOND ROUND) © OECD 2026

510. The allocated official is required to send an acknowledgement to the requesting jurisdiction and ask for decryption details where relevant. Once the request has been successfully decrypted, the official must stamp all the received information using the confidentiality stamp (see paragraph 463).

511. Once the allocated official has received or decrypted the request, the request is validated using a standard checklist. The checklist requires the official to perform various checks, including completeness, by checking that the appropriate legal basis is quoted, the request is signed by the appropriate foreign competent authority and the information requested is foreseeably relevant. If the request is incomplete or the foreseeable relevance is not clear, a request for clarification must be sent within 14 days. During the review period, Namibia sent out requests for clarification in the two bulk cases (see paragraph 497). These requests for clarification were justified. If all the aspects of the request are clear, the allocated official must prepare a validation checklist within five days for review and approval by the head of the EOI unit.

512. When the request has been accepted as foreseeably relevant, the allocated EOI official works on the request. If the requested information can be gathered from the internal NamRA databases and tax files, the EOI manual recommends that the associated request be responded to within 30 days. In other instances, if the complete information has not been gathered within 60 days, partial information should be sent to the requesting jurisdiction.
Verification of the information gathered

513. The gathered information is verified by the allocated official, who prepares a verification checklist as part of the process of preparing a response to the requesting jurisdiction. The official checks that all the requested information has been provided, and copies of documents attached (where relevant).

514. The Namibian officials reported difficulties to accurately validate the information against NamRA's records in the bulk requests received in 2022. In such cases, the validation process is manual, and the requests in question involve 6 939 individuals.

515. The draft answer explains whether all the requested information has been collected or whether the current response is a partial response. The confidentiality stamp is appended to all the documents.
516. The draft answer is reviewed and signed off by the head of the EOI unit. Peers expressed satisfaction with the information received from Namibia.
Outgoing requests
517. Namibia relies on outgoing EOI requests for its own audits and tax investigations. During the review period, Namibia sent five requests for information to its treaty partners.

518. The process for initiating an EOI request begins when a tax auditor or investigator identifies the need for information from another jurisdiction during an audit or investigation into potential non-compliance or tax risk. The requesting unit then contacts the EOI unit, after which an initial meeting is convened to review the facts of the case and assess whether the request has sufficient merit.

519. Following this meeting, the requesting unit completes the standard outgoing request template provided by the EOI unit. This template requires the presentation of relevant facts, the applicable legal basis, taxpayer details, the rationale demonstrating foreseeable relevance, and confirmation that domestic means have been exhausted. The EOI unit reviews the completed template to ensure that the request is clearly articulated. Once the EOI Unit has completed its review and the request has been finalised, it is securely transmitted to the requested jurisdiction.
520. Peers have been generally satisfied with the quality of requests sent by Namibia and found them to be generally foreseeably relevant.

521. Upon receiving the requested information, the EOI unit forwards the received information securely, indicating the treaty nature of the received information, and applies the confidentiality stamp. All competent authority communications are kept securely within the EOI unit.

522. There are no legal or practical requirements in Namibia that impose unreasonable, disproportionate or unduly restrictive conditions for EOI.

text: Convention on Mutual Administrative Assistance in Tax Matters (as amended)

The Convention on Mutual Administrative Assistance in Tax Matters was developed jointly by the OECD and the Council of Europe in 1988 and amended in 2010 (the Multilateral Convention). $^{24}$ The Multilateral Convention is the most comprehensive multilateral instrument available for all forms of tax cooperation to tackle tax evasion and avoidance, a top priority for all jurisdictions.

The original 1988 Convention was amended to respond to the call of the G20 at its April 2009 London Summit to align it to the standard on exchange of information on request and to open it to all countries, in particular to ensure that developing countries could benefit from the new, more transparent environment. The Multilateral Convention was opened for signature on 1 June 2011.

The Multilateral Convention was signed by Namibia on 29 September 2020 and entered into force on 1 April 2021 in Namibia. Namibia can exchange information with all other Parties to the Multilateral Convention.

Peer Review on Transparency and Exchange of Information on Request NAMIBIA 2026 (Second Round)
The Global Forum on Transparency and Exchange of Information for Tax Purposes is a multilateral framework within which over 170 jurisdictions participate on an equal footing.

The Global Forum monitors and peer reviews the implementation of the international standards on transparency and exchange of information on request (EOIR) and on automatic exchange of information. The EOIR provides for international exchange on request of information foreseeably relevant to the administration or enforcement of the tax laws of a requesting party. All Global Forum members have agreed to have their implementation of the EOIR standard assessed by peer review. In addition, non-members that are relevant to the Global Forum's work are also subject to review. The legal and regulatory framework of each jurisdiction is assessed, as is the implementation of that framework in practice. The final result is an overall rating of the compliance of the jurisdiction with the standard.

The first round of reviews was conducted from 2010 to 2016. A second round of reviews started in 2016. Peer reviews are generally conducted in one go, but they can be conducted in two separate reviews, with a Phase 1 reviewing the legal framework, followed by a Phase 2 focussing on practice. Reviews are phased when jurisdictions have limited EOIR experience or in exceptional circumstances, such as the COVID-19 pandemic. The review reports are published and assessed jurisdictions are expected to follow up on any recommendations made. The ultimate goal is to help jurisdictions to effectively implement the standard of transparency and exchange of information on request for tax purposes.

This peer review report analyses the practical implementation of the standard on transparency and exchange of information on request (EOIR) for Namibia, as part of the second round of reviews conducted by the Global Forum since 2016.
